The U.S. Navy contracted RTX to produce more than 1,900 Standard Missile-6s over five years in a $24.4 billion deal announced on Thursday.

“This SM-6 award gives industry the demand signal and stability to expand production, strengthen the munitions industrial base, and build the magazine depth our fleet needs. That is the foundry delivering for the fleet – and ensuring our sailors have the combat power to fight and win,” Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle said in a Navy release on the award.

While RTX and the Navy did not specify the amount of SM-6s that will be procured in the deal, a Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Munitions LinkedIn social media post graphic said that upwards of 1,900 missiles are covered through the deal. According to an RTX release, the contract provides the Navy with a consistent and reliable supply of SM-6s.

Described by its manufacturer as “three missiles in one,” the SM-6 has been selected by American forces to carry out air defense, air-to-air and surface-to-surface missions across a variety of platforms in recent years. The recently awarded five-year-long contract also has provisions for a two-year extension option.

“The SM-6 contract establishes a multi-year procurement commitment that provides industry with the stability and predictability needed to expand production capacity while delivering cost savings through a negotiated, long-term agreement. The investment will support increased manufacturing throughput and strengthen the industrial base supporting this critical capability,” reads the Navy release.

The procurement represents a significant munition purchase exceeding pre-Iran conflict stocks of the SM-6. According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington-based think tank, American stockpiles of the SM-6 were estimated to amount to 1,160 missiles before the conflict with Tehran began on Feb. 28.

The contract also comes after RTX was awarded several smaller contracts that prioritized the modernization of the SM-6 production line via increased automation and streamlining. In February, the Pentagon announced an award to bolster RTX’s ability to build several types of air defense, air-to-air and cruise missile. Among these advanced munitions, the February announcement highlighted the SM-6 lines increase to produce up to 500 missiles annually.

Beyond its presence aboard the Navy’s guided-missile destroyers, SM-6 has been integrated onto F/A-18E/F fighters and the Army’s ground-based Typhon containerized Mark 41 vertical launching system. Naval aviators can carry four of the missiles in the air-launched configuration AIM-174B aboard their carrier-based aircraft to field what a Navy fact sheet described as “unprecedented area defense capabilities.” The ground service wants to use the missile in a maritime strike role in support of a broader area denial mission against Chinese and Russian naval forces.

The Pentagon doubled down on its plans to establish a forward-deployed area denial, anti-access network along the First Island Chain to deter China in the 2026 National Defense Security update.

In a Sept. 22 report to the Senate Armed Services Committee on the 2026 NDS, Defense Under Secretary for Policy Elbridge Colby highlighted the department’s efforts to establish a “deterrence by denial” posture in the Indo-Pacific against China. The move is the culmination of attempts within the last decade to prepare American forces for a potential conflict against China, one that would require expansive logistics and missile volleys over the vast distances of the Pacific.

“We are also doing so through force development, as shown in our budget requests to Congress, which increasingly focuses on the kinds of conventional capabilities required to sustain deterrence by denial along the [First Island Chain],” reads Colby’s report.

The report said Colby wants to achieve the second-most important policy of the NDS, which aims to “Deter China in the Indo-Pacific Through Strength, Not Confrontation,” through similar methods via a first island chain denial plan.

Capabilities such as ground-based mobile missile launchers, stand-in forces, naval mines and sustainable aerial forces were emphasized in Colby’s statement. These contrast a previous reliance on large scale naval forces and reflect the Pentagon’s new approach to countering Chinese forces.

During previous contingencies in the region, such as the Taiwan Strait Crises, Washington relied on its fleet of aircraft carriers and forward-deployed air assets to deter China. However, with the modernization and expansion of Beijing’s Air Force and Navy, the U.S. is looking to the same area denial tactics, technologies and methods that China pursued decades ago to defend against blue water forces.

The effectiveness of holding large, conventional navies – such as what the People’s Liberation Army Navy is working to field and expand – under threat with unmanned surface vessels and coastal defense cruise missiles was recently demonstrated in the Black Sea, Red Sea and Strait of Hormuz.

In May, American special forces sank a ship in the Luzon Strait with a Ukrainian Magura drone loaded with an explosive warhead, USNI News previously reported. Meanwhile, U.S. Marine missileers deployed low-observable anti-ship missiles on the Philippine territories of Batanes and the Japanese Ryukyu Islands. When supported by longer-range missile systems such as the Tomahawk and SM-6 missile-equipped Typhon launcher, also known as Mid-Range Capability, these systems can create multilayered networks covering strategic waterways. The NDS update highlights Typhon launches and deployments to the Philippines and Japan.

Marine Corps and Air Force fighters are practicing dispersed operations across the First and Second Island chains. Both services demonstrated massed and long-range maritime strikes from their aircraft and bombers over the course of the summer. This year, the Air Force revealed that their B-2 Spirit stealth bomber has the capability to strike maritime targets with stealthy cruise missiles during an exercise in the Mariana Islands.

To back this posture, Colby said that U.S. forces are working to develop hardened command and control, the ability for sustained logistics in contested environments and the necessary magazine depth for anticipated munition expenditures required for an area denial posture in the first island chain.

In regards to the missiles needed to combat China in a potential conflict, Colby said that a high-low mix was needed for the needs of the Indo-Pacific and other contingencies.

“Rather than a false choice between exquisite munitions or low-cost, the Department recognizes we need both high-end munitions and munitions specifically designed to be rapidly producible in large quantities,” reads the report.

Within the last year, the Pentagon has announced several multi-billion dollar deals for more missiles and expanding production capacity of the defense industrial base. Thousands of low-cost and legacy missiles for air defense and strike missions have been procured. This week saw the Pentagon contract RTX for more than 1,900 Standard Missile 6 missiles in a deal worth up to $24 billion.

The following is a summary of major ship movements and exercises in the Western Pacific over the last week.

In the Malacca Strait

Destroyer USS Carl M. Levin (DDG-120) transited north through the Malacca Strait on Tuesday. The destroyer transited the Singapore Strait the day before. Carl M. Levin is now operating in the Indian Ocean. Homeported in Hawaii, Carl M. Levin is forward deployed and assigned to Destroyer Squadron (DESRON) 15

In Singapore

Royal Navy offshore patrol vessel HMS Tamar (P233) is docked in Singapore for maintenance.

Tamar and sister ship HMS Spey (P234) will participate in the Five Power Defense Arrangement (FPDA) exercise Bersama Lima, which runs from Oct. 12-21. The exercise will take place around the waters and airspace of Malaysia and Singapore. Both Tamar and Spey have been forward deployed to the Indo-Pacific since 2021.

Near Scarborough Shoal

The PLA Southern Theater Command ran readiness drills around Scarborough Shoal on Sunday and Wednesday. Sunday’s drills included a PLAN Jiangdao-class corvette, PLAN fleet oiler CNS Qinghaihu (885) and a WZ-7 Soaring Dragon Unmanned Aerial Vehicle being deployed, according to a video released by the command. A second video shows the Soaring Dragon UAV and a People’s Liberation Army Air Force KJ-500 airborne early warning and control aircraft taking off as PLAN frigate CNS Tongliao (554) and corvette CNS Tianman (631) operate in the area. 

A video of Wednesday’s drills shows a pair of PLAAF J-16 fighters escorting a PLAAF H-6 bomber over Scarborough Shoal and a KJ-500 AWEC flying separately over the shoal as PLAN frigate CNS Bayannur (551) patrols the area. 

Philippine Navy frigate BRP Antonio Luna (FFG-15) was monitored by a PLAN warship. Footage of a Philippine Air Force (PAF) F-27 Maritime patrol Aircraft, a Philippine Coast Guard C-208 aircraft and a Pa-31 aircraft was overlaid with audio from PLAN frigate CNS Yulin (569) warning the PA-31 that China held undisputable sovereignty over Scarborough Shoal and its adjacent waters. 

“The so-called award of the South China Sea Arbitration Case is an illegal, invalid piece of waste paper. Any claims or actions made by your side based on such ‘award’ will be null and void,” the video said.

The drills were in response to the ADMM PLUS Maritime Security Joint Cooperative Activity held in Subic Bay near Scarborough Shoal from Sept. 20-26.

In the South China Sea

Royal New Zealand Navy fleet oiler HMNZS Aotearoa (A11) carried out a replenishment-at-sea evolution with Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force helicopter destroyer JS Ise (DDH-182) on Saturday in the South China Sea. Both ships previously participated in the ADMM PLUS Maritime Security Joint Cooperative Activity. 

Saturday’s refueling was the first time Aotearoa has refuelled a JMSDF ship. 

Ise returned Wednesday to its homeport of Sasebo, Japan. Aotearoa with frigate HMNZS Te Mana (F111) form the Royal New Zealand Navy Task Group and are currently on deployment in South East Asia.

On Sunday, Royal Canadian Navy frigate HMCS Regina (FFH334) joined Aotearoa, Te Mana and Royal Australian Navy frigates HMAS Stuart (FF153) and HMAS Perth (FFH157) for a joint replenishment-at-sea in the South China Sea. Regina is on deployment under Operation Horizon, the Canadian Armed Forces’ ongoing presence and engagement deployment to the Indo-Pacific. Stuart and Perth are on separate Regional Presence Deployments, the Australian Defense Force’s annual deployment in the Indo-Pacific.

In Tanjung Priok, Indonesia

The Russian Navy Pacific Fleet surface action group docked Wednesday in Tanjung Priok, Jakarta, for a port visit until Sunday. The surface action group includes destroyers RFS Marshal Shaposhnikov (543) and RFS Admiral Tributs (564) and fleet oiler Pechenga. The strike group left Sept. 10 from Vladivostok for an Asia Pacific deployment.

Italian Navy multi-purpose combat ship ITS Giovanni delle Bande Nere (P434) also arrived Wednesday at Tanjung Priok, Jakarta, for a port visit until Monday. Giovanni delle Bande Nere is homeward bound following its Indo-Pacific deployment.

In Benoa, Bali 

RAN destroyer HMAS Sydney (DDG-42) docked Sunday in Benoa, Bali, for a port visit. Sydney is on the end leg of a deployment that saw it participate in the Rim of the Pacific (RIMPAC) 2026 and Pacific Dragon 2026 exercises in Hawaii and exercise Pacific Vanguard 2026 in Guam.

In Kijing Port, West Kalimantan, Indonesia

Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force amphibious tank landing ship JS Kunisaki (LST-4003) and three Japan Ground Self-Defense Force CH-47 helicopters completed their mission combatting forest fires in Indonesia on Tuesday.

In Tacloban City, Philippines

The U.S. Navy-led humanitarian and disaster preparedness mission Pacific Partnership 2026 (PP26) concluded its final mission stop in Tacloban City, Leyte, Philippines, on Monday. PP26 ran from June 1 to Sept. 29. The mission included stops in Vietnam, Indonesia, Timor-Leste, Malaysia and the Philippines, in addition to two enduring efforts in Fiji and Palau, reads a Navy news release. 

In the Philippines on Sept. 21, 376 service members from the U.S. and partner nations, including Canada, Germany, Japan, New Zealand, and the United Kingdom, collaborated with the Armed Forces of the Philippines to conduct more than three dozen activities along four lines of effort: engineering, disaster management, host nation outreach events and medical.

In Guam

Destroyer USS Wayne E. Meyer (DDG-108) departed Saturday from Naval Base Guam having made a short visit on the same day. Wayne E. Meyer, homeported in Pearl Harbor, Hawaii, is forward deployed and assigned to DESRON 15.

In Saipan

Destroyer USS Benfold (DDG-65) pulled into Saipan over the weekend, arriving on Saturday and departing on Sunday, according to a report by NMI News Service. Benfold, homeported in Everett, Wash., is forward deployed and assigned to DESRON 15.

In Okinawa, Japan

Amphibious transport dock USS San Diego (LPD-22) and Littoral Combat Ship USS Canberra (LCS-30) docked on Thursday in White Beach Naval Facility, Okinawa, Japan, for a port visit. Prior to docking, Canberra carried out Navy-Marine integration training with a Marine Corps AH-1Z Viper helicopter, attached to Marine Light Attack Helicopter Squadron (HMLA) 367, landing on its flight deck.

In Yokosuka, Japan

Cruiser USS Robert Smalls (CG-62) departed Saturday from Commander, Fleet Activities Yokosuka for a permanent homeport change to San Diego. The cruiser conducted mooring operations offYokosuka on Sept.24 and the following day sailed south through the Uraga Channel, which connects Tokyo Bay with the Sagami Gulf and Pacific Ocean, according to local ship spotters.

The corvette subsequently sailed northeast between Yonaguni Island and Iriomote Island to enter the East China Sea on Saturday and then headed to the Tsushima Strait. 

JMSDF fleet oiler JS Towada (AOE-422) shadowed the Russian corvette while it sailed in the vicinity of Yonaguni Island. Fast attack craft JS Shirataka (PG-829) shadowed Rezkiy while it transited through the Tsushima Strait, according to a Japan Joint Staff Office release.

The Navy brought in at least 45,112 active-duty enlisted sailors in Fiscal Year 2026, according to the sea service’s final numbers, released Thursday.

The Navy announced in July that it met its recruiting goal of 45,000, three months ahead of schedule, USNI News previously reported. It exceeded the goal by 112 sailors.

The sea service will now aim to bring in 45,000 more sailors in Fiscal Year 2027, which began Thursday, according to a Navy release. The new goal is 9,000 more than the Navy budget’s books, released in April, listed.

The Navy projects an end strength of 356,600 for FY 2027, an increase of 3,780, according to the budget books.

The Navy did not release numbers of how many officers the service commissioned in FY 2026 or its goal for FY 2027.

The sea service begins its next recruiting challenge with 13,508 future sailors in the delayed entry program pool, which is a population of recruits who will not immediately ship out to boot camp.

Rebuilding the DEP pool is a focus for the Navy, Rear Adm. Jim Waters, flag matters director, told USNI News in August. Waters turned over Navy Recruiting Command to Rear Adm. Forrest Young on Aug. 7.

The Navy wants to enter Fiscal Year 2028 with 50 percent of recruits in DEP, Waters told USNI News.

Young took over the command after the Navy had already reached its FY 2026 goal. He told USNI News in a Wednesday statement that he is taking time to speak with recruiters and sailors to find out what is working at Navy Recruiting Command.

“The recruiting environment will continue to evolve, and so will we – whether that means refining how we use data, improving the tools and training we provide recruiters, reducing friction in the applicant process, or finding better ways to connect with the talented Americans our Navy needs,” Young said in the statement. “Ultimately, every improvement we make should help our recruiters succeed and ensure we are delivering the right people, with the right skills, to the Fleet.”

Three warships were recently decommissioned as Fiscal Year 2026 came to a close on Wednesday.

The Navy bid farewell to Whidbey Island-class dock landing ship USS Germantown (LSD-42 and Ticonderoga-class guided missile cruisers USS Lake Erie (CG-70) and USS Shiloh (CG-67). 

The 40-year-old Germantown decommissioned on Sept. 24 during a ceremony held in San Diego. Germantown was the first dock landing ship to conduct Landing Craft Air Cushion amphibious operations and served during Desert Shield, Desert Storm, Operation Iraqi Freedom and Operation Enduring Freedom. Germantown also carried out humanitarian and disaster relief missions following the 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines, the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan as part of Operation Tomodachi.

“To the current and former crews, you are the heart and soul of this ship,” Cmdr. Benjamin Pearlswig, final commanding officer of Germantown, said during the ceremony. “A warship is nothing without the warfighters who walk their decks, that stand the watch and answer the call.” 

Shiloh was formally decommissioned Wednesday at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawaii, after 34 years of service as the Navy continues to phase out the Ticonderoga-class cruisers from the fleet.

Shiloh was among the first cruisers to launch Tomahawk land attack missiles into Iraq during Operation Desert Strike in 1996 and again during Operation Iraqi Freedom in 2002. In early 2005, the cruiser deployed in support of Operation Unified Assistance, to provide humanitarian assistance to communities affected by the Dec. 26, 2004, tsunami off the coast of Aceh, Indonesia, stated the release.

Shiloh also spent 17 years as a forward-deployed naval ship, having arrived in Yokosuka, Japan, in August of 2006. 

“The greatness of the ship was achieved by and delivered by three decades of sailors who embraced the ship’s name and heritage, and handed them off to everyone in the next generation,” said Rear Adm. Sharif Calfee, commander, U.S. Naval Forces Korea, and Shiloh’s 17th commanding officer. “We truly made the magic happen on the deckplates, every day.”

Cruiser USS Lake Erie (CG-70) decommissioned on Friday after 33 years of service during a ceremony in San Diego.

Lake Erie played a leading role in the development and operational testing of the Aegis Ballistic Missile Defense system, including several first-of-its-kind intercepts of ballistic missiles, the Navy said in a news release. 

The cruiser supported Operation Southern Watch in 1995 in addition to the withdrawal of peacekeepers in Somalia during Operation United Shield that same year. In February 2008, Lake Erie intercepted and destroyed a 5,000-pound errant U.S. satellite in Operation Burnt Frost. In 2017, Lake Erie participated in Operation Inherent Resolve conducting escorts through the Strait of Hormuz.

Lake Erie most recently deployed to the Caribbean to counter illicit maritime activity as part of Operation Southern Spear. Lake Erie concluded its final deployment in June after 11 months in the U.S. 4th Fleet area of operations. 

Also decommissioned this year were Los Angeles-class submarine USS Alexandria (SSN-757) on June 29 and Freedom-class Littoral Combat Ship USS Fort Worth (LCS-3) on July 29. Military Sealift Command also saw the inactivation of three replenishment oilers, two roll-on/roll-off ships and one of two of the Navy’s offshore petroleum distribution system ships in 2026. ships. The inactivations included: USNS Watkins (T-AKR-315) on July 1, USNS Pomeroy (T-AKR-316) on May 21, USNS VADM K.R. Wheeler (T-AG-5001) on May 29, USNS John Ericsson (T-AO-194) on July 31, USNS Pecos (T-AO-197) on July 31 and USNS Big Horn (T-AO-198) on March 31. 

 

Los Angeles-class submarine USS Newport News (SSN-750) and Watson-class vehicle cargo ship USNS Red Cloud (T-AKR-313) were slated to be decommissioned in 2026 but have had their active service extended. 

The decommissioning of Lake Erie and Shiloh leaves the Navy with five cruisers in service – USS Robert Smalls (CG-62), USS Princeton (CG-59), USS Gettysburg (CG-64), USS Chosin (CG-65) and USS Cape St. George (CG-71). 

The Navy extended the service life of three cruisers, Gettysburg, Cape St George and Chosin, which completed the cruiser modernization plan. The extensions added a cumulative total of 10 years of service from fiscal years 2026-29. Gettysburg, Chosin, Princeton and Robert Smalls are set to be decommissioned in FY 2027 and Cape St. George in FY 2028, according to the Navy’s Shipbuilding Plan. 

Princeton is deployed in the Indian Ocean while Chosin deployed this week with the Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group, according to the USNI News Fleet and Marine Tracker. Cape St. George is in its homeport of San Diego and Gettysburg in its homeport of Norfolk, Va..

Robert Smalls departed Saturday from Commander Fleet Activities Yokosuka for what is expected to be the final time. The cruiser is shifting homeports to San Diego ahead of its decommissioning next year. 

“This is our sayonara, leaving Japan for the last time” Capt. Francisco Garza, commanding officer of Robert Smalls, said in a news release. “This crew, and the crews that came before us on this hull, earned the trust of our Japanese partners and of the strike group. We leave proud of that record and grateful for the time we had in Yokosuka. Freedom through Courage.”

The cruiser was originally named USS Chancellorsville (CG-62) but was renamed in 2023 to honor a former slave who was conscripted into Confederate service in 1862. Robert Smalls, a skilled navigator, stole the steamer CSS Planter and escaped from Charleston on May 13, 1862, with his family, rescuing enslaved people and capturing military material. He turned the ship over to the U.S. Navy.

The departure ends 11 years of being forward-deployed to U.S. 7th Fleet. Robert Smalls was replaced by destroyer USS Mustin (DDG-89), which arrived on March 23 and is currently deployed in the Indian Ocean.

“USS Robert Smalls has been a vital part of our forward deployed force,” Rear Adm. Jeffrey Heames, commander of CSG 5 and Commander, Task Force 70, said in the release. “She is the last cruiser to leave Japan. Her sailors stood the watch here for more than a decade and strengthened our alliance every day they were on station. We thank them for their service and thank Japan for its partnership and hospitality.”

Five companies were selected to deliver prototypes of a missile capable of hitting moving, long-range maritime targets to the U.S. Army, the ground service announced Tuesday.

Anduril, Castelion, Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control, Mach Industries and RTX were awarded through five Other Transaction Authority agreements to develop and deliver their pitches for the ground service’s Precision Strike Missile Increment 4 program. The defense contractors are expected to deliver prototypes within Fiscal Year 2027 and receive follow-on contracts depending on their performance by FY28.

Increment 4 prototypes “must be operable in the Indo-Pacific Area of Operations,” according to a request for solutions document covering the PrSM variant released in May. PrSM Inc 4’s planned range also enables the Army’s new HIMARS-equipped Indo-Pacific multi-domain commands to disperse along island chains to hold vessels under threat.

Lockheed Martin has already been contracted for the first two increments of the missile program. Increment 1 is the base variant succeeding the ground branch’s Cold War-era Army Tactical Missile System. Between FY25 and FY32, the Army wants to receive 1,000 PrSM Inc 1s annually. To bring ground-based anti-ship missile capabilities to the service’s M142 High Mobility Rocket Artillery Systems, PrSM Inc 2 utilizes the same missile but integrates a seeker capable of tracking mobile maritime and ground targets.

Last month, Lockheed Martin was awarded $1.2 billion to deliver the first Inc 2 missiles to the service.

Castelion was contracted last year to fit its Blackheard hypersonic missile on HIMARS. The missile start-up is currently on contract with the Navy to integrate its low-cost hypersonics on F/A-18E/F carrier-based fighters. A containerized system carrying Blackbeard will be demonstrated aboard Saronic’s Marauder Medium Unmanned Surface Vessel by 2027, according to a joint release with the drone shipbuilder.

Compared to Inc 2, PrSM Inc 4 is an extended-range variant meant to be fielded in the Indo-Pacific to counter China’s expansive naval forces. To counter Chinese naval movements and amphibious assaults during a potential conflict, the Army has turned to the development of missiles designed to strike warships that can be fielded on the HIMARS.

These launchers can be deployed to the difficult terrain found across the First Island Chain, particularly those within the strategic straits separating Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines. In recent years, the U.S. Army, Marine Corps and Air Force have jointly trained to sail and fly in HIMARS to remote islands across the Indo-Pacific. Balikatan 2026 saw at least four deployments of the mobile American missile launchers within and near the Luzon Strait.

item.content:encoded:
The following is the Sept. 29, 2026, Government Accountability Office report, Coast Guard: Additional Action Needed to Address Marine Firefighting Challenges.

From the Report

Fires on vessels are extremely dangerous and difficult for firefighters to respond to. In 2023, a marine vessel fire resulted in the deaths of 2 firefighters.

After this, the U.S. Coast Guard worked to address firefighting risks—but it could do more.

For example, the Coast Guard works with local port officials, land-based firefighters, and others to make plans before fires occur. But it doesn’t always have dedicated local coordinators to lead those efforts. Training for land-based firefighters is also limited, e.g., not having hands-on exercises on vessels.

Our recommendations address these and other issues to improve marine firefighting efforts.

What GAO Found

Fires on vessels are among the most dangerous and challenging incidents to which firefighters can respond. Vessels may also carry hazardous cargo, like lithium-ion batteries, further complicating marine firefighting responses. According to U.S. Coast Guard data, there were 886 nearshore marine fires that occurred between 2015 and 2025. About one quarter (206) of these resulted in either death, injury, over $200,000 in damage, or a total loss of the vessel.

The U.S. Coast Guard is the principal federal agency responsible for overseeing marine safety. For marine firefighting, the Coast Guard plays a coordinating role while land-based fire departments extinguish fires. Following a marine fire that resulted in two firefighter deaths in 2023, the Coast Guard established a task force to address various marine firefighting challenges. The task force has taken several steps to address them but gaps remain.

Designating consistent Coast Guard field personnel to lead coordination before marine fires occur, facilitating more hands-on training for firefighters on vessels, and establishing an information sharing mechanism would help ensure firefighters have the knowledge and skills necessary to safely and effectively extinguish vessel fires. Further, developing guidance on what warrants vessel response plan activation would help ensure resources are quickly mobilized and better ensure the safety of firefighters.

The number of vessels that use alternative fuels continues to grow. However, legal limitations prevent the Coast Guard from requiring nontank vessels that use alternative fuels—such as ferries powered by lithium-ion batteries—to have vessel response plans related to hazardous substance discharges. These limitations predate the widespread use of alternative fuels. Having that authority would empower the Coast Guard to better ensure vessels and firefighters can quickly receive assistance in the event of a fire.

Why GAO Did This Study

The Coast Guard has issued regulations requiring certain vessels to have response plans that identify the resources that would respond to marine fires related to oil discharges.

The National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 includes a provision for GAO to review, among other things, the Coast Guard’s efforts related to marine firefighting. This report examines (1) how frequently nearshore marine fires occur and the characteristics of those fires and (2) what challenges exist in marine firefighting and how the Coast Guard is addressing them.

GAO analyzed Coast Guard data for 2015 through 2025; reviewed Coast Guard guidance and investigative reports; and interviewed Coast Guard officials, fire chiefs based in seven Coast Guard sectors, and representatives from maritime and firefighting stakeholder associations.

Recommendations

Congress should consider amending existing law to ensure that owners and operators of non-tank vessels that use alternative fuels prepare vessel response plans related to hazardous substance discharges.

GAO is also making five recommendations to the Coast Guard, including to designate marine firefighting coordination responsibilities to specific field positions, engage with fire departments to coordinate training, establish a mechanism to store and share marine firefighting information, and develop factors maritime stakeholders and the Coast Guard should consider regarding vessel response plan activation. The Coast Guard agreed with all five recommendations.

item.content:encoded:
The following is the Sept. 25, 2026, Government Accountability Office report, Naval Shipyards: Complete Information Needed for Decision-Making on Multibillion-Dollar, 50-Year Infrastructure Program.

From the Report

The Navy is taking on its largest-ever construction and restoration effort to improve poor conditions and outdated infrastructure at its 4 shipyards. These shipyards are essential to ensuring the Navy’s aircraft carriers and submarines are fit to fight in operations. This effort could take over 50 years and ultimately cost more than $200 billion.

But we found that Navy and congressional oversight requirements don’t include regular evaluation of costs, risks, and performance for this effort. Having such information for decision-making would ensure that current plans evolve with the Navy’s future needs.

Our recommendations address this and more.

What GAO Found

The Navy’s Shipyard Infrastructure Optimization Program (SIOP) will surpass $200 billion and take over 50 more years to execute, based on GAO’s analysis of Navy plans. Developing the plans and cost estimates to rebuild the Navy’s four public shipyards has taken the Navy years longer—and will cost much more—than originally anticipated due to multiple challenges and changes involved in the program. For example, environmental issues led to additional projects and more extensive work affecting project plans and costs at the shipyards, including Puget Sound Naval Shipyard.

The Navy established an oversight framework to guide SIOP plans and decisions over the duration of the program. The framework includes tools and requirements typically used for major defense acquisition programs—like for missiles, aircraft, or ships. However, the Navy has not outlined steps in the framework to reevaluate program objectives and resources as the program progresses over the next several decades. Without building such reviews into key future decision points, the Navy is limiting its ability to ensure that capabilities in SIOP’s plans today continue to be aligned or adjusted to support future fleet warfighting needs.

Further, while the Navy provides Congress with reports and briefings on various aspects of SIOP, the Navy does not provide Congress with consolidated, standardized information on full program costs and risks because there is no requirement to do so. In contrast, major defense acquisitions are required to provide annual program status reports with detailed metrics, including total costs to date, cost and schedule baselines, and risks, to track and monitor progress. Without a full picture of how much has been spent, what remains to be funded, and what risks may affect SIOP progress, Congress could make consequential decisions for SIOP based on incomplete information, thus risking billions in taxpayer dollars and a lack of program oversight for the decades to come.

Finally, the Navy created several organizations to manage SIOP projects and challenges. For example, the Navy created organizations for project oversight and program integration teams to coordinate issues with shipyards. However, the Navy has not fully documented the organizations’ roles and responsibilities. Doing so would formalize their new SIOP roles and help to ensure not only their ability to effectively implement SIOP’s essential projects but also the continuity of the critical shipyard operations to maintain and modernize the U.S. naval fleet now and throughout SIOP’s extended timeline.

Why GAO Did This Study

The Navy’s four public shipyards are essential to maintaining and modernizing the U.S. fleet of nuclear-powered vessels and its critical warfighting capabilities. The Navy initiated SIOP in 2018 to address poor shipyard conditions and capability gaps affecting fleet readiness. GAO has reported on the shipyards’ persistently poor condition and found that preliminary SIOP cost estimates were understated by billions of dollars.

The joint explanatory statement accompanying the Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2024 includes a provision for GAO to report on SIOP oversight and management. This report examines (1) Navy planning and implementation of SIOP, including costs, timing, and challenges; (2) Navy oversight of SIOP; and (3) Navy establishment of project management organizations to oversee SIOP construction projects.

GAO analyzed SIOP program documents and project cost and schedule data; visited the shipyards to observe SIOP projects and ship maintenance; and interviewed officials.

Recommendations

GAO recommends Congress consider requiring the Navy to annually report consolidated, standardized status updates for SIOP, including total costs, for its duration. GAO is also making three recommendations for the Navy to include future reviews of program requirements and resources in its oversight framework, and to document key SIOP organizations’ roles and responsibilities for managing shipyard projects and risks. The Navy agreed with the recommendations and outlined planned steps to implement them.

item.content:encoded:
This story has been updated to correct the spelling of USS Klakring (FFG-42). 

The U.S. Navy and Royal Navy sunk decommissioned frigate USS Klakring (FFG-42) earlier this month as part of a sinking exercise with Royal Navy forces.

Newly commissioned Virginia-class submarine USS Massachusetts (SSN-798) dealt the final blow to Klakring, sending it to the bottom of the Atlantic Ocean. Massachusetts fired an Mk48 Advanced Capability Torpedo at Klakring during the Sept. 20 exercise, sinking the decommissioned frigate around 150 miles off the northwest coast of Scotland. Massachusetts was commissioned in March and was declared ready for fleet tasking in August.

As part of the sinking exercise, Klakring was also the target of a Standard Missile 6 firing, a surface ship-launched Naval Strike Missile and a helicopter-launched Sea Venom missile.

The U.S. Navy and Royal Navy sunk the decommissioned frigate during the U.S. 6th Fleet-led Atlantic Thunder 2026, which ran from Sept. 14-25. Klakring entered U.S. Navy service on Aug. 20, 1983, and was decommissioned March 22, 2013.

“This sinking exercise not only validated the power behind U.S.-U.K. offensive weapons but delivers a clear message to adversaries that the U.S. Navy and Royal Navy remain a ready allied force,” U.S. Navy Capt. Kelechi Ndukwe, Commander, U.S. Task Force 65, said in a news release.

Participating in the sinking exercise were forces assigned to Commander, Task Force (CTF) 65, CTF 67, CTF 68, CTF 69 and CTF1060 alongside the Royal Navy and the U.S. Air Force. Involved ships and aircraft were Massachusetts and U.S. destroyer USS Paul Ignatius (DDG-117), Royal Navy frigate HMS Portland (F79) and its embarked Wildcat helicopter from 815 Naval Air Squadron, U.S. Navy and Royal Air Force P-8 maritime patrol aircraft, a Royal Navy Wildcat helicopter, U.S. Air Force F-15E Strike Eagle fighters and personnel assigned to U.S. Explosive Ordnance Disposal Mobile Unit 8.

The SINKEX saw the Royal Navy’s Portland fire its surface ship-launched Naval Strike Missile and helicopter-launched Sea Venom missile at Klakring, validating the missiles’ striking capabilities. Paul Ignatius also fired an anti-surface variant of the Standard Missile 6 at maximum range.

Paul Ignatius’ SM-6 firing was meant to test the furthest range for surface-to-surface engagement, Ndukwe said during a Monday media roundtable. He was unable to release the range distance. The SM-6 missile’s range is classified with estimates ranging from between 300-400 kilometers, or 186-248 miles.

Portland’s NSM firing during the exercise was the first firing of an operational NSM by the Royal Navy, according to a release from the service. Similarly, the firing of the Sea Venom was the first firing of an operational missile against a realistic target.

“The successful firing of NSM marks a significant milestone for the Royal Navy, demonstrating our ability to deliver credible, modern maritime strike capability,” said Lt. Cmdr. Louise Kirkaldy, Portland’s Principal Warfare.

During the exercise, the Wildcat crew completed the full “kill chain” process of detecting, identifying and striking the target, the Royal Navy said.

“This was a landmark moment for the Wildcat Force. For the first time we demonstrated the live firing of an operational Sea Venom missile against a representative maritime target. More importantly, we proved our ability to execute the full maritime strike kill chain under realistic operational conditions,” said Lt. Cmdr. Rhydian Edwards, Test & Evaluation Commander, Maritime Aviation Strike Operational Advantage Group.

He added that the firing will give commanders confidence that Wildcat can find, fix and strike maritime targets using Sea Venom as part of a wider task group and that the lessons learned from the activity will directly inform future tactics. Sea Venom reached Initial Operating Capability last year with Wildcats deployed with the U.K. Carrier Strike Group during the strike group’s Operation Highmast deployment.

The NSM will be a complementary weapon for the “Future Cruise Anti-Ship Weapon,” which will become the Royal Navy’s premier long-range, heavy duty anti-ship missile, carried by the service’s next-generation warships fitted with the Mk41 vertical launch system.

The NSM was introduced to Royal Navy service in 2023 to replace the phased out Harpoon missiles on its Type 23 frigates and Type 45 destroyers. Progress has been slow with only three frigates fitted with NSM and one of those frigates withdrawn from service this year. HMS Somerset (F82) was fitted with the missile in December 2023, Portland in December 2024 and HMS Richmond (F239) in February 2025. In July, the Royal Navy announced Richmond will be decommissioned.

Klakring is the fourth decommissioned U.S. Navy ship to be sunk in a SINKEX this year. Its sinking follows that of decommissioned amphibious transport dock USS Juneau (LPD-10) on June 27, decommissioned cruiser USS Mobile Bay (CG-53) on July 11 and decommissioned amphibious assault ship USS Peleliu (LHA-5) on July 17.

The Navy Shipbuilding Plan released in May lists 10 decommissioned ships slated for use in Rim of the Pacific, Valiant Shield and Atlantic Thunder sinking exercises during the Future Years Defense Program (FYDP) including the four ships already sunk. The six other ships include: cruisers USS Antietam (CG-54), USS Vella Gulf (CG-72) and USS Port Royal (CG-73), destroyer USS Paul F. Forster (DD-964), frigate USS De Wert (FFG-45) and amphibious dock landing ship USS Germantown (LSD-42).

In the case of Klakring, prior to the start of the exercise, Naval Surface Warfare Center Carderock and Naval Information Warfare Center Pacific used sensors placed on the ship to perform battle damage assessments. The data gathered will be used in post-exercise damage assessments to provide information to rapidly identify system failures, determine repair needs and strengthen the Navy’s future real-world response, reads the U.S. Navy release.

item.content:encoded:
MANILA, PHILIPPINES – The U.S. will transfer three King Air turboprop planes equipped for maritime domain awareness operations to the Philippine Coast Guard, the Pentagon announced Monday.

Technology Service Corp. was awarded $39 million for the procurement and integration of intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance kits onto King Air 350 Extended Range aircraft, reads the contract announcement. Two of the three aircraft will receive the ISR hardware and software modifications. Work also includes training on the surveillance suites and operation of the planes.

While the contract did not detail the specifics of the provided ISR kits, Technology Service Corp. advertises its Sea Dragon maritime domain awareness kit for integration aboard the King Air aircraft. The Virginia-based firm describes the product as a low-cost ISR system that can “enable local law enforcement to better protect national exclusive economic zones.”

This aircraft transfer was previously finalized in February following a meeting between Defense Department Undersecretary John Noh and Philippine Coast Guard Commandant Adm. Ronnie Gavan. Additional transfers to the Philippine maritime security agency announced this year include five ex-U.S. Coast Guard cutters, including one 210-foot Reliance-class.

The move is Washington’s latest effort to bolster Manila’s intelligence collection capabilities amid increasing tensions with Beijing over disputed maritime features in the South China Sea. Philippine forces have previously received U.S. transfers of unmanned surface vessels and patrol boats that have been used to monitor and track Chinese forces.

Alongside these maritime transfers, the Pentagon has handed over several modified Cessna aircraft with ISR kits to the Philippine Air Force. These turboprops were originally transferred in the 2010s for counterinsurgency operations. The Armed Forces of the Philippines have since shifted the aircraft to maritime patrol missions across the South China Sea in recent years to monitor Chinese forces.

Washington’s investments into developing Philippine ISR capabilities have been a key priority between the two nations. Until recently, the Philippine military has been almost entirely focused on internal security operations. The ongoing dispute in the South China Sea with Beijing – as well as concerns of a potential Taiwan contingency spilling over to the Luzon Strait – drives the Philippines’ push for modern defensive capabilities.

Aside from monitoring Chinese naval forces, Coast Guard and maritime militia operations off Palawan and Luzon, the American-supplied turboprops have been keeping the People’s Liberation Army Air Force busy over Scarborough Shoal. Media from the Chinese military’s Southern Theater Command frequently highlight the interception and tracking of Philippine military, Coast Guard and government turboprops flying over the disputed maritime feature.

On Wednesday, Chinese J-16 and JL-10 fighters supported by a KJ-500 airborne early warning and command aircraft tracked and monitored a Philippine turboprop aircraft over Scarborough Shoal. Chinese Type 054A frigates forward-deployed to the disputed area also practice air defense drills during Beijing’s combat patrols at the shoal.

Boeing will build the Navy’s next-generation fighter after decades of indecision on the future of the carrier air wing, according to a Tuesday Pentagon announcement.

“The contract is valued at more than $20B for the full-scale development phase. The contract procures multiple test aircraft for ground, airworthiness, systems, and weapons integration testing,” reads the announcement.

The new tactical aircraft is set to enter the fleet as the first Boeing F/A-18E/F Super Hornets leave the fleet in the 2030s. A primary mission for the new fighter will be to extend the effective strike range of the U.S. carrier air wing that has steadily shrunk over the last 20 years.

“The F/A-XX is a critical pillar in our commitment to maintaining peace through strength. F/A-XX will dominate contested airspace, extend operational reach, and deliver a decisive combat advantage for the warfighter,” Michael Duffey, Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition and Sustainment, said in a statement. “The F/A-XX platform represents a crucial, non-negotiable investment in America’s national security and long-term air combat capabilities.”

Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle said earlier this year the choice for the F/A-XX contract came down to the capacity of the builder.

“The Navy’s got a lot of demand… making sure that we don’t, again, fall into a trap of oversubscribing,” he said. “One of the contractors who would make this plane for us is in a place where they really can’t deliver in the timeframe we need it. So, there was a ‘check twice, cut once’ kind of mentality here on this decision.”

The sea service has shifted its position on what the role of the F/A-XX will be from a “missile truck” to a stealthy penetrator that would command swarms of armed drones against enemy air, land and sea targets as part of a next-generation air dominance from work that would create a “family of systems,” according to reports in USNI News over the last decade.

“This achievement marks a new era for the U.S. Navy,” said acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao. “The sixth-generation fighter is a generational leap in air superiority and will provide the world’s best aviators with unparalleled capabilities to fight, win, and come home safe. We are excited to partner with Boeing, and for our warfighters to continue to dominate the skies and defeat our nation’s enemies.”

In the last several years, the Navy has said little about the current requirements or detailed the cost of the program, only recently disclosing its asks for the program.

As part of the Fiscal Year 2026 defense budget, Congress approved $1.7 billion for the F/A-XX program, according to Pentagon budget documents.

In April, Caudle said the F/A-XX would fold in with the Navy’s naval collaborative combat aircraft (CCA) in which armed robot aircraft will carry out missions in tandem with manned aircraft.

“The CCA concept is all part of our sixth-generation concept. It’s tied with the overall air wing of the future concept,” he said. “It is a program that we’re working very hard trying to do that in learning with the Air Force on what CCAs look like in the future and the way we’re going to command and control those, how many, what’s the number that a pilot can reasonably control and task. AI is part of that.”

The Navy has four CCAs under contract from General Atomics, Boeing, Anduril and Northrop Grumman. In addition, Lockheed Martin is under contract to develop a ground control system. Earlier this month, the Navy submitted a request for information for additional CCAs.

Integration of the unmanned MQ-25A Stingray carrier tanker that is set to refuel the carrier air wing is also part of the Navy’s future air wing, but the development of the Boeing-built drone has faced production delays.

Naval analyst Bryan Clark with the Hudson Institute told USNI News on Tuesday the most important characteristic for the F/A-XX absent drone cooperation was range, and the Navy would have to balance that requirement with the size limitations of an aircraft carrier.

“For the Navy, the range constraints are significant. The Navy is going to have to have an aircraft that’s very efficient,” Clark said.

The Air Force announced its own sixth-generation air superiority fighter with a range of 1,000 nautical miles in a White House ceremony last year. According to Clark, a land-based fighter has some range advantages over a naval fighter.

“If you look at the F-47, it generates the range by just being big and having more gas in it,” he said. “They just make a bigger airplane.”

item.content:encoded:
Three Louisiana-based shipyards will build unmanned surface vessels for the U.S. Navy following recent at-sea testing, the service announced Tuesday. 

The three companies – Saronic, HII and Galliano Marine Service – will each build 10 medium unmanned surface vessels, or MUSVs, at about $40 million per hull, the Navy’s acting direct reporting portfolio manager for robotic and autonomous systems Chris Miller told reporters in a virtual roundtable. 

The Navy issued the awards using other transaction authorities but did not specify how much each company received. A service news release described the $40 million figure as an average cost per vessel. The funding comes from the reconciliation legislation known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act that Congress passed last year.

“The phase one production awards were based on the optimal mix of autonomy performance, design, production schedule and cost,” Miller said during Tuesday’s call. “The production will begin immediately at shipyards in Loreauville, Houma, and Franklin, Louisiana, with deliveries starting as early as the fourth quarter of [Fiscal Year] 2027.”

Miller was referring to the location of the three yards. Breaux Brothers, which is partnered with HII, is based in Loureauville, in Iberia Parish. HII is also working with Halimar Shipyard in Morgan City to build its Romulus MUSVs. Galliano Marine Service, which also does business as Edison Chouest, is based in Houma, La. Saronic is building in Franklin, La., at the yard formerly known as Gulf Craft that the company has poured hundreds of millions of dollars in for an expansion, USNI News reported. 

The Navy’s requirements for phase one called for a vessel that could travel for 2,500 nautical miles at 25 knots in sea state 4, while transporting payloads up to 25 metric tons across at least two 40-foot shipping containers.

The contract announcement comes after several weeks of at-sea testing that concluded this month. 

“The test was that they had to be able to execute roughly 26 hours in over 360 nautical miles with only a single input during that time from a [command and control] station allowed,” Miller said of the testing requirements. “It basically demonstrated that the vessel could run for an excess of 24 hours at an extended range with very minimal input from the actual operator from a C2 station.” 

The six companies that met the testing parameters will each receive $15 million and go into the Defense Department’s drone marketplace, Miller said.

Seven companies took part in the tests after making it to the prototype phase in May. In addition to the three companies that won the production awards, Birdon, Leidos, PacMar Technologies and Sea Machines also participated. Birdon is the only company that did not successfully meet the requirements.

Miller said Birdon has a “viable path” to get into the marketplace in the future as the Navy prepares for a second phase of the MUSV program.

“They really got a later start and I think if they had been given more time, they would have been able to successfully get there,” he said. “We will work with them and I want to help them be successful.”

Last week, the Navy put out a solicitation for MUSV phase two, which Miller said aims to bring more types of unmanned vessels into the marketplace.

“What I’m trying to do is also give more industry opportunities for companies that have something ready to go,” he said. “Obviously, with phase one, there were some more challenging requirements that they had to meet and so I’m trying to back off of those so that I can have a healthy, competitive industrial base and really use that to help us identify near-term opportunities to meet our operational demands.”

The service’s requirements allow for a wider variety of craft and require less payload. The vessel can be a maximum of 295 feet long and must be able to operate for 10 days and survive in sea state 6, according to a draft requirements document reviewed by USNI News. Noting that the high speed mandate for phase one led to some difficulties, Miller said phase two does not have a high-speed or refueling-at-sea requirement.

“The phase two solicitation allows entrants to compete and existing vendors to submit updated product blocks and modular payload configurations,” Miller said. “Testing evaluations will begin as early as November 16 and proposals will be assessed on a continually rolling basis over the next five years.” 

Miller declined to comment on the ongoing lawsuit that two other companies – Blue Water Autonomy and Saildrone – filed against the Navy following the prototype awards for phase one.

“We are prepared to handle whatever decision that the judge decides,” he said. “But I really don’t want to get into specifics of that ongoing litigation.”

The two companies claim the Navy did not follow its own selection criteria when picking the awardees.

item.content:encoded:
The future USS John F. Kennedy (CVN-79) achieved preliminary acceptance Tuesday, one of the last steps before it formally joins the fleet, as carrier USS Harry S. Truman (CVN-75) prepares for its mid-life overhaul.

JFK, the second Ford-class aircraft carrier, left Tuesday from HII’s Newport News Shipbuilding division to eventually transition to the waterfront at Naval Station Norfolk, Va., as part of the preliminary acceptance, according to an HII spokesperson.

The milestone allows the Navy and JFK’s crew to take the aircraft carrier to sea for underway testing and evaluation prior to official delivery to the sea service.

“Achieving preliminary acceptance marks a new phase for the ship and her crew, allowing them to get more water under the keel as they test and train underway,” Capt. Mark Johnson, the Navy’s Program Manager for Gerald R. Ford-Class New Construction, said in the Navy press release. “This milestone is a testament to the shared commitment of our sailors and our combined Navy-industry team, who remain laser-focused on completing the final stages of construction and test with precision and efficiency to deliver combat-ready lethality to the fleet.”

JFK is scheduled to deliver to the service in March, according to the Navy’s 2027 budget documents.

“Achieving preliminary acceptance is another step toward ensuring the U.S. Navy has the aircraft carriers it needs to carry out the mission of defending our nation,” Bryan Caccavale, NNS vice president of program management, said in a statement from HII. “It is an honor to see Kennedy depart and begin integration into the fleet.”

JFK completed acceptance sea trials in August with seven out of 11 Advanced Weapons Elevators having been delivered. The sea trials followed years of delays and Navy and congressionally mandated equipment changes to the ship, USNI News reported. Completing the AWE and the Advanced Arresting Gear were the two major barriers to delivery.

Now, JFK is approximately 99 percent complete, the Navy said in a Tuesday press release.

“All major systems are complete. The shipbuilder is currently completing final ship systems testing, including testing of the remaining four Advanced Weapons Elevators,” reads the Navy’s news release.

The preliminary acceptance comes as HII’s Newport News Shipbuilding prepares to receive Harry S. Truman. The Navy issued Newport News Shipbuilding a $5 billion contract for Truman’s refueling and complex overhaul, the Pentagon announced Tuesday. RCOH’s are comprehensive maintenance and modernization overhauls done at the midpoint of a carrier’s lifespan.

The overhaul will be a down-to-the-bulkhead refit of the 25-year-old carrier and will also top off the carrier’s two nuclear reactors. The RCOH will include extensive modernization work in thousands of compartments and tanks, as well as on most ship systems, reads the contract announcement. In addition, the propulsion plant and combat systems will receive major upgrades.

Work is expected to be completed by November 2031.

Newport News Shipbuilding received a $913 million advanced procurement contract for Truman’s RCOH in January of 2024. That work is set to be completed in 2026, USNI News previously reported.

“Our team has been diligently working to get ahead on this critical engineering and construction project that will prepare USS Harry S. Truman for the second half of her service life,” Caccavale said in a separate statement. “When the ship arrives at NNS, we’ll apply that same diligence to working with our suppliers and Navy partners to ensure a successful recapitalization of CVN 75.”

The Norfolk-based carrier has been in a pierside maintenance phase since returning from deployment in June of 2025.

Built at Newport News Shipbuilding, Truman was christened in 1996 and delivered to the Navy in 1998. Truman will be the eighth Nimitz-class carrier to undergo RCOH at the Virginia shipyard.

item.content:encoded:
The Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group quietly departed Monday from San Diego for a scheduled deployment, USNI News has learned.

Big-deck amphibious warship USS Makin Island (LHD-8), the flagship of the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group, was sighted sailing under the Coronado Bridge on its way out to the Pacific after 1 p.m. Monday local time. That same day, amphibious transport docks USS Anchorage (LPD-23) and USS John P. Murtha (LPD-26) also deployed from San Diego.

A Navy official confirmed to USNI News that the amphibious ships had deployed.

The three ships make up the Makin Island Amphibious Ready Group. An ARG/MEU typically includes about 2,200 Marines and sailors that are part of the MEU, and another approximately 2,000 sailors across the three amphibious ships.

— WarshipCam (@WarshipCam) September 28, 2026

The 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit is deploying with the Makin Island ARG. Over the last few months, Marines with the 13th MEU conducted integrated training with the three ships off the coast of California. That integrated training is part of the workups that ARG/MEUs do ahead of a deployment.

The 13th MEU’s Marine Air-Ground Task Force includes the Battalion Landing Team 2/4 and the Combat Logistics Battalion 13, according to Navy and Marine Corps media released in recent months. The aviation squadrons are Marine Medium Tiltrotor Squadron (VMM) 364 (Reinforced) and Marine Fighter Attack Squadron (VMFA) 211, which includes MV-22B Ospreys, AH-1Z Vipers and F-35B Lightning IIs.

The Boxer Amphibious Ready Group with their embarked Marines deployed from the West Coast in March, less than one month after the U.S. launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran. However, the group did not arrive in the Arabian Sea until early July, according to the USNI News Fleet and Marine Tracker.

As of Monday, the Boxer ARG was still operating in the Arabian Sea. The ARG includes Boxer, USS Comstock (LSD-45), USS Portland (LPD-27) and the 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit.

This post will be updated as new information becomes available.

Four personnel were injured in a landing mishap aboard USS Dwight D. Eisenhower (CVN-69) on Monday, USNI News has learned.

The two-person crew of an EA-18G Growler assigned to the “Zappers” of Electronic Attack Squadron (VAQ) 130 were safely recovered after ejecting from the aircraft, the Navy said in a statement provided to USNI News.

“At approximately 6:18 p.m. EDT on Sept. 28, a mishap involving an E/A-18G Growler, attached to the ‘Zappers’ of Electronic Attack Squadron (VAQ) 130, occurred during aircraft recovery operations aboard the Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Dwight D. Eisenhower off the coast of Virginia.“Two naval aviators assigned to Carrier Air Wing (CVW) 3 subsequently ejected from their aircraft following an arresting gear failure and were promptly recovered by search-and-rescue personnel assigned to Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron (HSC) 7. Both aviators were safely returned to the ship.”

Eisenhower is in the midst of early carrier qualifications after completing its most recent repair period in July. According to ship spotters, the ship left this afternoon from Naval Station Norfolk, Va.

The following is the complete update as of Sept. 29, 2026, from the U.S. Navy. 

UPDATE 1: At approximately 6:18 p.m. EDT on Sept. 28, a mishap involving an E/A-18G Growler, attached to the “Zappers” of Electronic Attack Squadron (VAQ) 130, occurred during aircraft recovery operations aboard the Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Dwight D. Eisenhower (CVN 69) off the coast of Virginia.

Two Naval aviators assigned to Carrier Air Wing (CVW) 3 subsequently ejected from their aircraft following an arresting gear failure and were promptly recovered by search-and-rescue personnel assigned to Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron (HSC) 7. Both aviators were safely returned to the ship.

A total of eight Sailors were evaluated by ship’s medical personnel following the incident. One Sailor was flown to a Norfolk-area hospital for treatment of non-life-threatening injuries. The two aviators and two additional Sailors injured on the flight deck were flown to Naval Medical Center Portsmouth for follow-on evaluation.

Our immediate priority is ensuring all personnel involved receive the care and support they need. Carrier crews regularly train for emergencies and unexpected situations during flight operations, and that training enabled the crew to respond quickly and safely.

The cause of the mishap is under investigation. Updates will be provided as additional information becomes available.

item.content:encoded:
The European Union is asking its members to increase the number of ships deployed with European Naval Force Aspides, which is tasked with accompanying merchant ships in the Red Sea to protect them from Houthi attacks.

“We need more vessels because literally there are commercial ships that are waiting in the queue to receive the escort that we do not have enough frigates that can do that,” EU High Representative Kaja Kallas said Monday, according to a transcript following a meeting of EU Defense Ministers held in Brussels, Belgium.

Aspides was launched in February 2024 to protect merchant shipping from attacks in the Persian Gulf, Red Sea and Northwest Indian Ocean. The mission consists of up to a three-ship taskforce made of rotational deployments from EU nations.

But over the past month, Kallas has been pressing for an increase in the number of ships contributed due to the “worsening situation” in the Red Sea. The Yemen-based Houthis resumed attacks on Saudi-linked ships in the Red Sea in July after announcing a maritime embargo on Saudi Arabia. Since then, the Houthis seized Perim Island, a parcel of land that gives the Iranian proxy group a strategic foothold over the Bab el-Mandeb, USNI News reported. 

Italy and Greece are the main ship contributors. Italian Navy frigate ITS Carlo Bergamini (F590), which is operating as the flagship for Aspides, is deployed for the mission. 

Italian Navy minehunters ITS Crotone (M5558) and ITS Rimini (M5561), currently deployed in Djibouti for Aspides, were ordered to return to Italy for maintenance and crew rotation, according to a Wednesday announcement from Italian Minister of Defense Guido Crosett. The two minehunters were included in the Aspides deployment to reduce response times for mine clearance in the Strait of Hormuz, Crosett said. The minehunters will be replaced by two similar ships. 

“This is a rotation of units, necessary to ensure the long-term efficiency, maintenance, and operational availability of our ships, without interruption in the activities carried out by Italy as part of the European mission,” Crosetto said.

Two unidentified countries have hinted that they would provide additional ships to escort merchant vessels, Kallas said Monday. However, the need is not just about the quantity of ships but also the type of ships – specifically frigates and air defense support are needed. 

“When Aspides was put in place, then the indication was that it needed at least 10 ships. The situation is even more grave right now, as we see increased attacks. Also we see that the Strait of Hormuz is closed. This is a vital waterway for the trade. So, I would assume that it is more than 10, but we do not have that much right now,” Kallas said according to a Sept. 21 transcript.

The Trump administration has argued that the Strait of Hormuz is open, while Iran claims it is closed. 

EU members have already pledged a number of frigates and destroyers to the Mediterranean in anticipation of a U.K. and French-led multinational mission to protect merchant vessels in the nearby Middle East in response to the ongoing conflict between the U.S. and Iran. 

The mission was spearheaded in April to conduct mine clearance operations in the Strait of Hormuz with the caveat that the mission would only begin when a sustainable ceasefire agreement was put into place. 

A ceasefire has yet to hold.

British, Dutch, Italian and German naval vessels that deployed to the Mediterranean and Red Sea are returning or have returned home as the mission commencement continues to remain in limbo. 

Royal Navy destroyer HMS Dragon (D53), Royal Netherlands Navy frigate HNLMS De Ruyter (F804) and minehunter HNLMS Willemstad (M864), Italian Navy minehunters ITS Crotone (M5558) and ITS Rimini (M5561) and German Navy fleet oiler FGS Mosel (A512) are concluding their deployments to the region. 

Ships deployed by the Netherlands and Italy are slated to return home but will be replaced, the countries announced.

Netherlands frigate De Ruyter set out on April 12 for a circumnavigation deployment called Pacific Archer 2026 that would see it pass through the Middle East, Indo-Pacific, Hawaii, Panama Canal and the Caribbean before arriving home in the Netherlands. On June 19, having departed Tokyo to head to Hawaii, the frigate was rerouted to the Strait of Hormuz for a potential deployment with the Multinational Military Mission. The frigate embarked a multinational staff in early August in preparation for the mission. 

The Netherlands, in May, also deployed minehunter HNLMS Willemstad (M864) to join Standing NATO Mine Countermeasures Group 2, a naval task force focused on mine countermeasures in the Mediterranean Sea. Willemstad was also made available to join the multinational mission.

De Ruyter arrived home on Sept. 22, having been replaced by frigate HNLMS Evertsen (F805). Willemstad is also slated to return home. 

“Whether and when the cabinet actually deploys the frigate in the Strait of Hormuz depends on developments in the security situation and political decision-making,” reads a Netherland Ministry of Defense news release. 

Evertsen will also support the EU missions Aspides and Atlanta when sailing through the relevant operational areas during its deployment, according to the release..

The Gibraltar Broadcasting Corporation (GBC) reported that Royal Navy destroyer Dragon docked in the naval base in Gibraltar on Saturday, seemingly en route to its homeport. 

Dragon deployed in March to defend Cyprus from Iranian drone and missile attacks as of a result of ongoing hostilities in the region. In early May, Dragon transited the Suez Canal to join the French Carrier Strike Group led by aircraft carrier FS Charles De Gaulle (R91), which was directed to head to the Middle East in anticipation of the multinational mission. 

On July 4, Macron announced that the French CSG would head home after the U.S. and Iran agreed on June 17 to a ceasefire. The ceasefire later crumbled. 

Two French Navy frigates and two minehunters stayed behind. Both frigates remain deployed in the region, according to the latest French Armed Forces Operational Status Update. According to the update, one frigate was made available on an ad-hoc basis to support EUNAVOR Aspides missions.

Dragon, on June 18, escorted Royal Navy mine countermeasures mothership RFA Lyme Bay (L3007), German Navy minehunter FGS Fulda (M1058) and fleet oiler FGS Mosel (A512) as they transited the Suez Canal to deploy for the Hormuz mission. The two German Navy ships stationed themselves at Djibouti.

The German Ministry of Defense announced on July 23 that Fulda and Mosel would redeploy to the Mediterranean. Maintaining forces in the region – given the volatile political situation, the unlikely short-term establishment of a permissive environment and the unpredictable timely start of operations – represented an avoidable strain on the ships, reads the release. 

Lyme Bay remains deployed with AIS data placing it north of Zanzibar, Africa. Ship spotters sighted Mosel and sister ship FGS Rhein (513) on Sunday docked in Rota, Spain. Both the German and U.K. Defense Ministries have not issued recent information on the status of deployments.

item.content:encoded:
Chinese forces rehearsed enforcing Beijing’s claim to Scarborough Shoal with drones and boarding drills on Sunday amid state media claims that China has extended its control of several contested maritime features beyond 24 nautical miles.

The People’s Liberation Army Southern Theater Command and China Coast Guard held consecutive exercises within and around Scarborough Shoal, which is 120 nautical miles west of the Philippine island of Luzon.

Chinese military forces publicly showcased the deployment of a Guizhou WZ-7 Soaring Dragon drone at Scarborough Shoal for the first time. Previously used drones, such as the CAIG Wing Loong II, were also used during the weekend’s training activities. A Shaanxi KJ-500H airborne early warning and command aircraft was highlighted in released media from the command. 

Type 054A frigates, a Type 056A corvette and a Type 908 replenishment vessel participated, according to the imagery. Additionally, helicopters and drones were launched from the warships.

Beijing’s expanded posture at Scarborough Shoal has involved a significant roster of advanced strike aircraft, guided-missile destroyers and surveillance platforms in recent years to counter Manila’s recent approach to the contested maritime feature, USNI News previously reported.

Chinese state media outlet Global Times reported the China Coast Guard conducted a boarding operation that simulated the interception of “a foreign ship intruding into territorial waters.” According to the report, China has extended its “control” of Scarborough and Second Thomas Shoals beyond 24 nautical miles.

“China’s legitimate control around [Scarborough Shoal] and [Second Thomas Shoal] has now extended beyond 24 nautical miles, while regular control has been established around [Sabina Shoal] and [Sandy Cay]. The scope of China’s control is continuing to expand. The more the Philippine side provokes, the stronger the China Coast Guard’s control measures will become,” reads the Global Times story.

According to maritime tracking data, China’s forward-deployed warships and cutters at South China Sea flashpoints such as Scarborough Shoal regularly intercept Philippine vessels around 30-40 nautical miles from the maritime feature. Beijing uses its expansive fleet of vessels and sensors to tag and track Manila’s efforts to counter Chinese territorial claims. Further tracking from the SeaLight Foundation shows that Chinese cutters shadow vessels as soon as they leave the 12 nautical mile territorial waters.

These Chinese state media claims coincide with the recent blocking of a Philippine resupply mission to BRP Sierra Madre (LT-57) at Second Thomas Shoal. Beijing said Manila did not properly clear the voyage under the yet to be disclosed provisional agreement between the two countries following the June 17 Incident of 2024. Friday’s encounter marked the first publicly revealed instance of a blocked resupply mission since the agreement was inked.

China claims that Sunday’s drills were in response to the Philippine-led ASEAN Defense Ministers’ Meeting – Plus maritime security exercise held last week. Eleven vessels from eight nations, including the U.S., Japan, Australia, India and Singapore, joined the Philippines for activities within the vicinity of Scarborough Shoal. The Philippines invited a shadowing Chinese frigate to join the drill, but received no response.

item.content:encoded:
Carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) quietly departed Sunday from San Diego to sail across the Pacific for what is expected to be an extended Middle East deployment, USNI News has learned.

The carrier, the flagship of Carrier Strike Group 9, departed without the traditional pomp and circumstance – no sailors were spotted manning the rails, according to ship spotter photos. The carrier will embark with Carrier Air Wing 11. A defense official confirmed Theodore Roosevelt had begun its planned deployment.

The Theodore Roosevelt Carrier Strike Group is expected to move to U.S. Central Command to relieve the Japan-based USS George Washington (CVN-73), which entered U.S. 5th Fleet in mid-August. West Coast-based strike groups have been diverted from their traditional Indo-Pacific deployments to the Middle East in recent years amid tensions with Iran and the Yemen-based Houthis.

Since Feb. 28, when the U.S. conflict with Iran began, the Navy has maintained a two-carrier presence in the region, as well as deployed an amphibious ready group and a dozen independent warships.

Master Chief Petty Officer of the Navy John Perryman said in August that Theodore Roosevelt families were planning for their loved one to be away from home for more than seven months, USNI News reported.

“[Sailors] will go do really hard things for me without really batting an eye because they like that part of it. But we do have to be able, when possible, to stick to schedules and be very honest, like we are with Roosevelt,” Perryman told reporters. “They know they’re going to be there longer than seven months. Their [commanding officer] is giving them eight months to plan on.”

Aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) spent more than eight months in the Middle East without the relief of a port call, USNI News reported. Lincoln, destroyer escort USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. (DDG-121) and the embarked Carrier Air Wing 9 were sailing near Hawaii en route to California on Sunday, a defense official told USNI News.

Petersen is expected to return to Pearl Harbor today.

Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao visited the carrier, according to photos posted on social media.

“Today, our warfighters aboard USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) demonstrated the overwhelming capacity and capability that they brought to bear on our adversaries for the last 10 months,” reads a Facebook post, shared late Sunday.

As of Monday, Lincoln has been deployed for 311 days.

Currently operating in the Middle East are two carrier strike groups – the GW and George H.W. Bush CSGs – and the Boxer Amphibious Ready Group, according to the USNI News Fleet and Marine Tracker.

item.title: HII FF(X) Patrol Frigate Program Progressing as Navy Considers Foreign Options
item.dc:creator: Sam LaGrone

VIRGINIA BEACH, Va. — Both U.S. and foreign designs for the next small-surface combatant are under consideration after the cancellation of the Constellation-class guided-missile frigate, the new head of the Navy’s shipbuilding enterprise said this week.

A foreign design study is running in parallel with the development of HII Ingalls’ FF(X) Flight I patrol frigate, which was announced late last year following the Constellation cancellation, Portfolio Acquisition Executive Rear Adm. Casey Moton told an audience on Thursday at the American Society of Naval Engineers Fleet Maintenance and Modernization Symposium.

Moton confirmed that the HII frigate had passed its critical design review (CDR) earlier this year, which had not been previously announced by the Navy, and was working with HII Ingalls Shipbuilding on the pre-production work. The Navy awarded a $282 million advanced contract for long-lead items in April.

“We just went through CDR on the Flight I, and so we’re doing some pre-production activities with HII to help prepare for that material,” he said.

PAE Maritime is also in the process of the mandated 90-day review of the foreign ship designs, working with “the other stakeholders within the Department of the Navy and [the Pentagon] and [the Office of Management and Budget] and others, talking about the various options, putting those together as part of the response to the presidential study,” Moton said.

The Navy will apply the “Finland Model” to small surface combatant construction in a similar manner as the Coast Guard’s acquisition of the Arctic Security Cutter, according to a White House memo issued in August. Under the model, yards are building Coast Guard hulls in Finland before transitioning construction to the United States with a major investment in U.S. shipbuilding.

Ships under consideration include the Japanese Mitsubishi Heavy Industries’ FFM Mogami-class guided-missile frigate and the South Korean Chungnam-class guided-missile frigate and the Istanbul-class guided-missile frigate, USNI News reported earlier this month.

Neither the Navy nor the White House has made it clear if the Navy will pursue two different classes of small surface combatants.

“In terms of which path we go – I’m not going to get ahead of that process – but [studying all options is] essentially what we’re doing,” Moton said. “I am not going to get ahead of what we are doing in response to the presidential memo.”

A senior Navy official told USNI News earlier this month all options for small surface combatants, including building both the Ingalls frigate and a foreign design, were on the table.

In addition to the foreign ship study and the HII frigate, Constellation shipbuilder Fincantieri Marinette Marine is prepared to build an export variant of the FREMM guided-missile frigate at its Wisconsin shipyards, CEO George Moutafis told USNI News this week.

Moutafis said the supply chain the shipyard built during the Constellation could be applied to Fincantieri’s FREMM EVO design with few modifications to avoid the design churn that led to the cancellation of the Constellation.

“Right now the Navy and the administration could find the right type of dialog with us to set [development] up in a way that enables quick setup and swift construction without letting design spirals get in the way,” he said. “Accept the design that is and works well, and start work on it to get units out there for the fleet.”

The Navy assessment of foreign designs is due to the White House on Nov. 12.
