WASHINGTON NAVY YARD – Navy shore infrastructure will be in failing condition by 2037 if the sea service continues to use its current funding schedule, the new deputy chief of naval operations told USNI News on Thursday. 

As the newly created deputy chief of naval operations of sustainment, Vice Adm. Scott Gray, who will report on Oct. 5, will be tasked with continuously pushing for funding for shore infrastructure, including barracks and piers. 

“The idea is to continue the efforts to revitalize the shore, make wise investments and kind of bring the shore infrastructure back to where it needs to be to better support the needs of the fleet,” Gray said. 

On Thursday, fighting back a cold and some tears, Gray relinquished his role as commander of Navy Installation Command. The newly promoted Vice Adm. Brad Collins assumed CNIC in a change of command ceremony at the Naval History Museum.

Gray will oversee Navy shore installations, logistics and maintenance, with Commander, Navy Installations Command, Naval Facilities Engineering Systems Command and Naval Supply Systems Command falling under his purview. 

The creation of the deputy chief of naval operations for sustainment is meant to enable faster decision making and support the fleet by increasing integration and accountability across Navy staff, Capt. Dave Hecht, a Navy spokesperson, told USNI News. 

Shore infrastructure has taken a hit over the years, especially in funding, Gray said. The ongoing war in Iran has damaged oversea bases and created logistical challenges, while structural changes in Navy equipment, like a heavier P-8 Poseidon, has led to new challenges for the aging infrastructure. 

“We’re struggling pretty mightily to keep our ships maintained, and that’s in a peacetime environment,” Gray said. 

Part of the maintenance backlog is the underfunding of shore infrastructure in recent decades. Gray compared it to owning a house. Skipping a repair doesn’t immediately hurt the home, but doing it again and again over 20 years will leave the house in disrepair. What would have cost $100 at the time is now a $20,000 problem. 

“The shore installation portfolio is very much in that situation. Because of the under investment, we’ve taken risk, and we’ve tried to balance that across the many parts of that portfolio. And as you do that over time, the material condition of it continues to degrade,” he said.

Piers, runways, dry docks all need to be revitalized, as do housing and food halls, Gray said. 

“There’s this natural tendency to move toward the things that are shiny, bright objects, [like] the airplanes,” he said. “But there are real challenges and impacts to our sailors and quality of life by degraded piers, by degraded facilities.”

Sailors adapt to the deficiencies that have come from the lack of funding, Gray said. Sailors load up ships instead of being able to use a crane because the piers don’t support them, he said. What could take four hours takes 10. 

“There’s just so many things like that in the shore enterprise, where we’ve just adapted and tried to overcome the deficiencies that we have and cumulatively what is happening [is it’s] adding up, and it’s impacting overall sailor quality of service,” Gray said. 

An advantage of the shore command is the ability to take risks, Collins said. The command can try a new approach, and if it doesn’t work, try something else.

One area that could be adapted is the ability to do more underway maintenance in order to prevent longer time in the shipyard after a deployment, Gray said. There also needs to be a discussion about what maintenance must be done and what could be put off so that the ship can get back to the fleet. 

“We often have the tendency to want to make everything perfect,” Gray said. “And it’s unaffordable. It drives longer maintenance periods, and we need to be able to say, to make compromises and to make smart decisions about the maintenance that we’re doing.”

As CNIC, Gray worked on infrastructure projects, which included quality of life initiatives that led to the recent funding of a new unaccompanied housing project for Newport News, Va., USNI News previously reported, and bringing free Wi-Fi to barracks. The Navy currently stands at 90 percent of barracks with Wi-Fi.

Other projects included working with Dominion Energy to bring power-grid improvements to Naval Air Station Oceana in Virginia, Coleen San Nicolas-Perez, Navy Installations Command public affairs deputy director told USNI News.

Collins will inherit the ongoing quality of life efforts under CNIC, prompted by the suicide deaths of sailors on USS George Washington (CVN-73) and at the Mid-Atlantic Regional Maintenance Center in 2022. This includes the Newport News barracks project and parking for the sailors whose ships are in the shipyard. 

CNIC, under Gray, also inspected all of the Navy barracks, closing five substandard facilities, Vice Chief of Naval Operations James Kilby said Thursday during the change of command. 

Quality of life initiatives are an ongoing challenge, Collins told USNI News ahead of the ceremony. As CNIC, he’ll be tasked with pushing the Navy to fund ongoing programs meant to get after such problems. 

The Navy previously moved money around to accomplish the quality of life initiatives, but going forward, there needs to be a longstanding commitment from the Navy for the programs and CNIC plans, Gray said. 

Gray is putting together a briefing for Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle that will lay out all of the infrastructure challenges in order to advocate for the appropriate funding. 

“If we’re going to make meaningful and lasting change, we have to have a commitment from the Navy to, first and foremost, recognize the scope of the problem, and then commit to a program that will […] over time – it’s not going to happen in a day, it’s not going to happen in a year, it’s going to be over a number of years – to commit to a curve that gets us on an upward slope across all of our shore infrastructure,” Gray said.

Chinese warships and cutters blocked a Philippine resupply mission to Second Thomas Shoal on Thursday in the most significant development at the disputed South China Sea feature.

The People’s Liberation Army Navy and China Coast Guard attempted to “hinder” the resupply mission, Manila’s National Task Force for the West Philippine Sea announced on Friday.

“In doing so, they put Filipino personnel at risk and obstructed a legitimate humanitarian and sustainment operation,” reads the task force’s statement.

Two Philippine Coast Guard patrol vessels, BRP Malabrigo (MRRV-4402) and BRP Cabra (MRRV-4409), were supporting the Philippine Navy-operated resupply ship Lapu Lapu when Chinese forces intercepted the resupply mission. According to a statement from the Philippine maritime security agency, the mission was temporarily suspended following “dangerous maneuvers” by the Chinese forces that threatened a collision with Lapu Lapu.

The incident occurred 60 nautical miles away from Second Thomas Shoal.

A graphic released by the Philippine Coast Guard shows three Chinese cutters shadowing Cabra and Lapu Lapu. An additional force of 11 China Coast Guard and China Maritime Militia vessels were observed near the Philippine Navy’s grounded World War II-era landing ship BRP Sierra Madre (LT-57) at Second Thomas and Sabina Shoals. The Armed Forces of the Philippines told local media outlet ABS-CBN News that the PLAN deployed three warships, including two Type 022-class missile boats, to support the interception of Manila’s vessels.

Sierra Madre has been a flashpoint in Manila’s territorial disputes with Beijing in recent years. Since 2022, Philippine and Chinese forces have engaged in an increasingly escalatory standoff involving dangerous maritime maneuvers, rammings, water cannons and a culminating clash in 2024.

After the culminating incident on June 17, 2024, Manila and Beijing inked a yet to be disclosed provisional agreement that enabled Philippine forces to access Second Thomas Shoal without harassment. Thursday’s encounter was the first publicly reported instance of China blocking a resupply mission since the agreement was put into practice in July of 2024.

The terms of the 2024 deal are not publicly available. Chinese state media outlet Global Times reported that this week’s incident occurred because the Philippines did not get approval from Beijing to sail to the shoal. Manila has repeatedly denied that the provisional agreement stipulates that Philippine forces require Chinese approval to access Sierra Madre.

The waters around Sierra Madre have become increasingly tense in recent months after Philippine and Chinese sailors engaged each other in a melee with batons and oars in July. Last year, armed Chinese small boats swarmed Second Thomas shortly after a fatal incident at Scarborough Shoal between the PLAN and CCG.

The resupply mission’s timing this week also coincided with a Philippine-led multinational maritime drill near Scarborough Shoal involving Association of Southeast Asian Nation member states and partners such as the U.S., Australia, India and Japan on Wednesday.

The following is a summary of major ship movements and exercises in the Western Pacific over the last week.

In U.S. 7th Fleet Area of Operations

The Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group (CSG) is underway following a two-day stop in Guam last weekend. The strike group includes aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72) with embarked Carrier Air Wing (CVW) and destroyer USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. (DDG-121). 

As of Friday, Abraham Lincoln has been deployed for 308 days.

In the Philippine Sea

Destroyer USS Carl M. Levin (DDG-120) is conducting routine operations in the Philippine Sea. Carl M. Levin is forward-deployed and assigned to Destroyer Squadron (DESRON) 15.

Destroyer USS Benfold (DDG-65) is operating in the Philippine Sea. Benfold, homeported in Everett, WA., is forward deployed and assigned to DESRON 15.

In the South China Sea

The Philippines and Japan are co-hosting the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defense Ministers’ Meeting-Plus (ADMM-Plus) expert working group on Maritime Security Joint Cooperative Activity , which began Monday and ends on Saturday.

The shore phase took place in Subic Bay, Zambales, while the sea phase began on Wednesday.

U.S. Navy participation includes Littoral Combat Ship USS Canberra (LCS-30) and a P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft (MPA). Other participating ships are Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force helicopter destroyer JS Ise (DDH-182), Indian Navy frigate INS Sahyadri (F49) and corvette INS Kulish (P63), Philippines frigate BRP Jose Rizal (FFG-14) and BRP Tarlac (LD-601), Royal Australian Navy frigate HMAS Perth (FFH157), Republic of Singapore Navy littoral mission vessel RSS Justice (18) Royal Brunei Navy offshore patrol vessel KDB Darussalam (06) and Royal New Zealand Navy frigate HMNZS Te Mana (F111) and fleet oiler HMNZS Aotearoa (A11). The ships formed a combined task group for the exercise.

Philippine media outlet ABS-CBN News reported Thursday that a People’s Liberation Army Navy warship shadowed the task group as it approached the designated exercise box, which was around 45 nautical miles from Scarborough Shoal. China is a member of the ADMM-PLUS group but only attended the opening ceremony of the exercise.

While in the South China Sea en route to the Philippines, the Royal New Zealand Navy task group of Te Mana and Aotearoa conducted a duel replenishment at sea with Royal Australian Navy destroyer HMAS Sydney (DDG42).

In Banten, Indonesia

Beginning on Monday, the ADMM-Plus Group conducted Exercise Trident in the province of Banten, Java, Indonesia. Trident Resolve is the first ADMM-Plus Combined Field Training Exercise involving three experts working groups on cyber security, Humanitarian Assistance and Disaster Relief and Military Medicine. Australia and Cambodia headed the cyber security group, Singapore and New Zealand headed the HADR group, and the U.S. and Indonesia headed the military medicine group.

Indonesia hosted the exercise. 

Trident Resolve is the largest ADMM-Plus exercise in a decade, according to a Singapore Ministry of Defense news release. Participation includes 2,200 personnel from all 19 ADMM-Plus countries. The exercise is being conducted across seven distributed sites and at sea. 

The exercise, which will conclude Saturday, has seen militaries and civilian agencies carry out coordination and response to a large-scale disaster, through activities spanning search and rescue, medical evacuation and treatment, chemical, biological and radiological response and infrastructure repair. Cybersecurity activities have focused on protecting information systems and information integrity against disruption or compromise during the multinational disaster response. 

The Indonesian Navy deployed hospital ship KRI dr. Soeharso (990) and the Republic of Singapore Navy deployed amphibious tank landing ship RSS Endeavour (210) for the exercise.

In Port Klang, Malaysia

Royal Navy offshore patrol vessel HMS Spey (P234) docked into Port Klang Cruise Terminal, Malaysia on Tuesday for a port visit, as well as for engagements with the Malaysian Armed Forces. 

Spey will depart next week to participate with sister ship HMS Tamar (P233) in Five Power Defence Arrangement exercise Bersama Lima, which runs from Oct. 12-21 around the waters and airspace of Malaysia and Singapore. Both Spey and Tamar have been forward deployed to the Indo-Pacific since 2021.

In Laem Chabang, Thailand

Italian Navy multi-role combat ship ITS Giovanni delle Bande Nere (P434) docked into Laem Chabang Thailand on Tuesday for a port visit, which will conclude Saturday, according to an Italian Embassy news release. Giovanni delle Bande Nere is on home bound following an Indo-Pacific deployment that saw it take part in the Rim of the Pacific 2026 and Pacific Dragon 2026 exercises held over the summer around Hawaii.

In West Kalimantan, Indonesia

JMSDF amphibious tank landing ship JS Kunisaki (LST-4003) and one Japan Ground Self-Defense Force CH-47 helicopter are supporting Indonesia in carrying out firefighting and relief operations against the ongoing wildfire in the province of Ketapang. Two other JGSDF helicopters that were embarked on Kunisaki remain at Kijing Port to conduct firefighting operations in the area around the port.

In Wonsan, North Korea

North Korea conducted hypersonic missile test launches on Sunday with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un overseeing the tests. Two missiles were launched towards the Sea of Japan with the first at 3 p.m. local time and the second at 5.50 p.m. local time.

Separately, state media Korean Central News Agency reported Thursday that North Korea’s defense scientific research sector conducted a test of updated 240mm-calibre controlled multiple-launch rockets. The updated rockets incorporated an autonomous precision guidance system and are capable of striking targets up to 100 kilometers 62 miles – away via ballistic flight and 115 kilometers – 72 miles – via a combined glide flight method. No location was given for the tests.

In Yokosuka, Japan

Fast attack submarine USS Scranton (SSN-756) departed Tuesday from Yokosuka, Japan, following a port visit, according to Japanese ship spotters.

In Hokkaido, Japan

The U.S. Army, JGSDF and Australian Army concluded exercise Orient Shield 26 on Thursday with a closing ceremony at Camp Higashi-Chitose, Hokkaido, Japan. 

Orient Shield 26 featured several firsts for the exercise, including the integration of tactical operations centers to create a shared common operational picture at the tactical level, enhancing coordination and information sharing among participating forces, reads a U.S. Army news release. 

The exercise also featured its first joint airborne operation, with approximately 260 U.S. soldiers parachuting from five C-130J Super Hercules aircraft. U.S., Japanese and Australian forces also participated in rigorous field training and multinational maneuver operations, including firing the High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS), while the JGSDF fired their Multiple Launch Rocket System during a live-fire event on Tuesday at Yausubetsu Training Area, Hokkaido.

In La Pérouse Strait, Japan

At 5 a.m. on Wednesday, Russian Navy cruiser RFS Varyag (011) and missile range instrumentation ship Marshal Krylov (331) were sighted sailing northeast 60 kilometers – 37 miles – west of Rebun Island and subsequently sailed east through La Pérouse Strait to enter the Sea of Okhotsk. JMSDF fast attack craft JS Kumataka (PG-827) shadowed the Russian ships.

In the Sea of Japan

On Friday, a Russian IL-20 Electronic Intelligence (IL-20) flew in from the Russian continent and over the Sea of ​​Japan to the west coast of Hokkaido. The aircraft then flew off Tottori Prefecture on the main island of Honshu before turning back towards Russia. 

In response, fighter aircraft from the Japan Air Self-Defense Force’s Northern Air Defense Command and other units were scrambled, stated Japan’s Joint Staff Office.

In Sydney, Australia

Fleet oiler HMAS Supply (A195) returned Wednesday to Fleet Base East, Sydney, Australia, following a 101-day deployment across the Indo-Pacific. During the deployment, it visited Singapore, Japan and the Philippines and worked alongside regional partners, including the U.S and Philippine navies. 

“Supply’s integration with the US Indo-Pacific logistics command, Task Force 73, demonstrated the high level of interoperability between the Royal Australian Navy and U.S. Navy, enabling allied and partner forces to operate together effectively through shared logistics, maritime sustainment and cooperative activities,” reads an Australian Defense Department news release.

This post was written by Dzirhan Mahadzir.

VIRGINIA BEACH, Va. — Not quite two months on the job, a submariner turned head of the Navy’s vast maintenance operation promised his office would create a more nimble organization that would better balance risk to speed ships back to the fleet.

Program Acquisition Executive for Industrial Operations Rear Adm. Todd Weeks told a crowd of ship maintainers the service wants to reduce the barriers to get ships out of maintenance on time.

“We absolutely need to change, and we’re not getting it done. We just aren’t,” Weeks said Thursday while speaking at the American Society of Naval Engineers Fleet Maintenance and Modernization Symposium. “We’ve got to be better than we are and we [have] got to focus on what is it going to take to deliver the ship, the submarine, the aircraft carrier out of maintenance.”

PAE IO is now in charge of the Navy’s major maintenance efforts including the 38,000 civilian maintainers across the four public shipyards and contracting with private repair yards for surface ship maintenance. The Navy’s public yards are largely responsible for fixing nuclear submarines and carriers while the surface Navy’s amphibious warships, cruisers and destroyers are maintained and modernized in a network of private yards across the country.

Maintenance trends have not been positive.

Over the last decade, the Navy has seen increasing delays in the maintenance of its destroyers and amphibious warships by 20 to 100 percent depending on the ship, according to a Congressional Budget Office report from December.

Likewise, 15 attack submarines are projected to enter idle status between 2026 and 2030 due to overall availability of maintenance capacity, and only 11 percent of public yard maintenance for submarines were completed on time, according to an August Government Accountability Office report.

Private shipyards responsible for the Navy’s surface work have long complained the service is not delivering a steady supply of work, is slow to issue contracts and change orders and often fails to deliver government furnished equipment for availabilities on time.

Capt. Tim Moore, who has overseen the Destroyer Modernization 2.0 for the last three years, said on Wednesday that delays in contracts and material from the Navy to shipyards were the top two bottlenecks in getting private yards to deliver on time.

“We don’t always do a good job with that and still expect them to finish on time… while we’re waiting on material to be delivered,” he said.

The Navy’s maintenance effort was – until this year – nested under Naval Sea Systems Command. A Pentagon-wide reorganization of responsibilities broke out several of the functions into PAEs who report to the Assistant Secretary of the Navy for Research, Development and Acquisition, according to the March implementation memo.

Weeks, a career submariner, was initially tasked to head new submarine construction under the Navy’s submarine czar Vice Adm. Robert Guacher but was moved to PAE IO earlier this summer.

Weeks’ mandate now is to get ships back to sea following repair yards.

“My view of this is that if we’re doing this right, we have sort of a semi-frictionless plane that allows us to move the people, the money, the capacity, to where we need it,” he said. “Where the fleet commanders say, ‘This is my number one priority. This is what I need you to do for me.’ We can swarm to that, deliver the right capability at the right time to be able to get the maintenance outcome that the fleet commander and our Navy need.”

Part of the effort will be to be more comfortable with risk rather than the Navy’s traditional mindset of overanalysis, he said.

“I just need to know enough to be able to make a good decision. That’s it, and there’s risk inherent to that,” Weeks said. “We have to embrace that. We have to recognize that that’s the world we live in today.”

“We’re really good at driving technical risk to zero and shifting all this operational risk back to the fleet,” he continued. “No, we’re out of that business now.”

“For example, at the request of the operational commander, the PAE IO trimmed four months off a public yard availability for a submarine through direct conversations over the risk of curtailing some of the repairs,” Week said.

“My mandate was we’re going to make the decisions in this room. There’s no… ‘We’ll get back to you in a month or six weeks.’ No, we’re going to do it now,” he said. “We all get the outcome we want, which is the submarine delivered in 25 months instead of 29.”

Weeks’ comments come one day after Navy leaders said that the service’s long-term commitment to maintaining a major naval force in the Middle East for the foreseeable future has already altered how the service thinks about supply and maintenance.

“The traditional model of naval ship maintenance is no longer viable in this high-demand operational environment,” U.S. Fleet Forces commander Adm. Karl Thomas said Wednesday. “That’s what we [have] got to change.”

The U.S Navy recently demonstrated that an autonomous aircraft can receive a mission plan and execute that mission as part of the Collaborative Autonomy Mission Planning (CAMP) tool, the service announced Tuesday. 

CAMP is meant to integrate autonomous aircraft with mission planners, helping the two communicate in a common way. Mission planners develop the overall mission – including what each aircraft should do, when it should do it, and what authorities and limitations apply in the Collaborative Mission Planning Continuum (CMPC) – and then CAMP translates that information into a format an autonomous aircraft can use to carry out its assigned role as part of a larger battle plan, reads the Navy news release.

“CAMP is about making autonomy more usable by integrating into mission environments with both manned and unmanned platforms,” said Capt. Todd “Toby” Keith, PMX-281 program manager. “This demonstration showed how we can connect the way operators plan missions today in the CMPC with the way autonomous aircraft will execute those missions. That can reduce the burden on our operators, improve interoperability and help bring collaborative autonomy closer to operational use.”

The demonstration was carried out by a team from Naval Air Systems Command’s Strike Planning & Execution Systems (PMX-281) on Sept. 10 during the Gray Flag 2026 exercise held at the Point Mugu Sea Range, Calif. PMA-281 is responsible for the acquisition and life cycle management of mission planning, control systems and execution tools that are developed and integrated in partnership with other NAVAIR program offices, other military services and foreign nation partners, according to the NAVAIR’s webpage.

During the exercise, an MQ-20 Avenger from General Atomics Aeronautical Systems acted as a surrogate aircraft, receiving the mission plan and executing the mission. The results are being reviewed. The MQ-20 Avenger, which General Atomics officially calls the Predator C Avenger, is a jet-power derivative of the company’s Predator drone.

PMX-281, managed by the Program Acquisition Executive for Munitions, is supporting the Navy’s development of mission-planning capabilities that define aircraft roles, tasks, timing, authorities and constraints. CAMP builds on that work by connecting those plans directly to autonomy-enabled aircraft.

The connection provided through CAMP will make it easier for the Navy to integrate different autonomous aircraft and systems into future operations. The tool also allows mission planners to focus on the operational objective rather than having to translate plans into different platform-specific formats. CAMP is also supporting the Navy’s broader goal of developing interoperable autonomy systems as autonomous platforms operating together require a common way to exchange mission information. Through CAMP, a connection is provided between mission-planning systems and the specific information an individual aircraft needs to perform its role, stated the release.

Additionally, CAMP builds on the Navy’s Experimental Platform for Intelligent Combat (EPIC) effort, which has demonstrated autonomous vehicle control, mission behaviors and coordinated operations using surrogate aircraft in live, virtual and constructive environments.

General Atomics was selected by NAVAIR’s PMA-281 for the Collaborative Autonomy Mission Planning and Debrief (CAMP) project, according to an April 20 announcement. 

The CAMP project will demonstrate the potential for extending PMA-281’s Mission Planning Software framework to support behavioral tasking, Rules of Engagement (ROE) configuration, AI decision thresholds, and comprehensive mission debrief capabilities, General Atomics said.

According to General Atomics, the CAMP project will demonstrate key capabilities on the MQ-20 Avenger platform equipped with Government Reference Implementation autonomy, Electronic Warfare and Infrared Search and Track payloads and features Link 16, Tactical Targeting Network Technology and Starlink satellite communications. 

Demonstrations are meant to highlight how mission planning software enables behavioral tasking, Electronic Warfare (EW) and Infrared Search and Track employment, combat air patrol, and target engagement, with execution and coordination demonstrated via Link 16-enabled platforms including F/A-18 Super Hornets, General Atomics said.

Additionally, the Navy announced on Sept. 14 that it had awarded a $562 million Fixed Price Incentive contract to Boeing for the MQ-25A Stingray Lot 1 Low Rate Initial Production (LRIP). The award provides the funds for three LRIP Lot 1 MQ-25As and additional funding for the advanced acquisition of long lead components to support three LRIP Lot 2 MQ-25As. Initial deliveries from Lot 1 are expected to begin in 2029.

The MQ-25A program of record includes 76 air vehicles, four Engineering Development and Manufacturing and five System Demonstration Test Articles. Currently, seven test aircraft are in production at Boeing’s St. Louis, Ill., location and the dedicated MQ-25 production facility in Mascoutah, Illinois.

The Navy has been conducting various trials using Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA), notably in December 2025 and January. General Atomics, Boeing, Anduril and Northrop Grumman are on contract for the conceptual design of the Navy’s CCA with Lockheed Martin under contract to build the common control system, USNI News previously reported. 

NAVAIR was seeking industry feedback and capability statements for the Navy Collaborative Combat Aircraft Increment 1 Prototype Project – specifically seeking information on an affordable, highly capable, risk tolerant, carrier-capable, weaponized, extended range, autonomous unmanned air vehicle that can deploy from and recover to Gerald R. Ford-class and Nimitz-class aircraft carriers – according to an Aug. 31 RFI. The RFI closed on Sept. 18.

“This RFI solicits industry expertise for the development and evaluation of two fully functional, unmanned autonomous prototype air vehicle(s) achieving shorebased carrier certification requirements within three (3) years or less from agreement award. The prototypes must be designed to meet full carrier qualification requirements and employment in HCE (Highly Contested Environments) aboard CVNs, while also possessing the flexibility to operate from austere locations with minimal infrastructure,” reads the RFI.

The Navy’s affordability goal for the CCA was at $30 million per unit. The CCA solution must feature reconfigurable weapon payload carriage to execute strike missions and both internal and external weapon carriage designs will be considered, with capacity and survivability being driving factors in design evaluation. The CCA must have the ability to carry four weapons up to 2,500 pounds each externally throughout the target flight envelope and carrier certification flights.

Companies were required to provide the maximum combat radius including weapons loadout, 30 minutes on-station and reserve fuel for safe recovery that their proposed CCA can perform and that the CCA must be able to organically reposition to a carrier in contested environments, operate from expeditionary locations without significant infrastructure additions to a carrier in the contested environment or join a carrier-launched mission. The CCA must also be able to operate at the cruise speed of a carrier and must not take up space on a carrier exceeding existing 4th generation fighter aircraft. 

The first flight is targeted at 24 months after contract award.

The following is the Sept. 23, 2026, Congressional Research Service report, Bahrain: Issues for U.S. Policy.

From the Report

The Kingdom of Bahrain is a small island nation connected by a causeway to Saudi Arabia (15.5 miles away) and once claimed by Iran (124 miles away). Wedged between these two larger regional powers, Bahrain has hosted a U.S. naval command headquarters since 1948. For decades, Bahrain has permitted U.S. access to its facilities and has hosted U.S. Naval Central Command (NAVCENT) and the U.S. Fifth Fleet at a base called “Naval Support Activity (NSA) Bahrain.” NSA Bahrain has long served as the logistical hub for U.S. maritime operations in NAVCENT’s area of responsibility and has hosted thousands of American soldiers, civilians, and their families.

Since the ongoing conflict between the United States and Iran began in February 2026, Bahrain’s security and economy have faced unprecedented challenges from Iranian retaliatory attacks against the island kingdom. To date, Iran’s drone and missile strikes have struck both Bahrain’s critical infrastructure and U.S. military facilities. As of fall 2026, numerous reports indicate that NSA Bahrain sustained serious damage in the opening days of the conflict. With NSA Bahrain damaged, U.S. Naval logistics operations have faced an array of challenges.

Congress routinely reviews proposed U.S. arms sales to Bahrain, and Bahraini procurement of additional advanced protection systems to counter incoming missiles and drones from Iran may accelerate in the months and years ahead. Congress also annually authorizes military construction funding for NSA Bahrain, which may require substantial repair in the near future. Preliminary reports indicate that damage to NSA Bahrain from Iran attacks is estimated to be at least $400 million. P.L. 119-60, the National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for Fiscal Year 2026 authorized $42 million in military construction for maintenance and facility upgrades at NSA Bahrain. For FY2027, draft NDAA bills would authorize $5.9 million in energy programs for NSA Bahrain.

Bahrain is ruled by a hereditary monarchy and is a member of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC; Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Qatar, and Oman); its politics have been restive, though the monarchy’s control has not been durably threatened. With a population of 1.5 million people, a little over half of whom are Bahraini citizens, Bahrain has a history of sectarian tensions between the Sunni Muslim ruling class and the Shia Muslim majority: Bahrain is the only GCC state to have a Shia majority population. Bahrain’s politics were unsettled during a 2011 uprising by a mostly Shia opposition to Bahrain’s Al Khalifa ruling family; a Saudi military intervention helped Bahrain’s government repress protests. Since 2014, the unrest has been relatively low-level. Several senior opposition leaders remain imprisoned.

Bahrain closely aligns with de facto GCC leader Saudi Arabia, which provides Bahrain with substantial financial support. Bahrain, like some other GCC states, has been building ties to Israel and, in September 2020, Bahrain signed agreements at the White House to fully normalize its relations with Israel as part of the “Abraham Accords.” During the war between Israel and Hamas, Bahrain and Israel did not sever relations, though some Bahrainis have protested bilateral ties.

Members of Congress have traveled with some frequency to Bahrain to visit U.S. armed services personnel and provide oversight over the U.S. bilateral relationship and defense presence in the kingdom.

NEW IBERIA, Louisiana – Surrounded by rows of sugar cane fields on Bayou Teche, generations of shipbuilders are wrenching on the U.S. Navy’s latest push toward a future drone fleet.

Work boat builders and repair facilities dot U.S. Route 90 in southern Louisiana, where the boom and bust of the oil and gas industry looms over yards small and large. It’s along this road where several shipyards are vying for a chance to build unmanned ships for the world’s most powerful navy.

At Breaux Brothers Enterprises outside of Lafayette, La., four aluminum Romulus vessels are currently under construction for a collaboration agreement between the yard and HII, the United States’ largest shipbuilder.

Breaux Brothers has built high-speed vessels for the petroleum industry since the 1940s, when Brannon Breaux’s grandfather started building aluminum crew boats in Iberia Parish.

“Undoubtedly, my family’s name – Breaux – has built more crew boats from the 40-something to 200-foot [range] than anybody else in the world,” Breaux, the president of Breaux Brothers and a third-generation boat builder, told USNI News over boudin and cracklins on a muggy morning visit in August.

Breaux Brothers and yards like it in central Louisiana construct offshore support vessels, the pickup truck of the oil and gas industry. Yards built them by the hundreds during the height of the Gulf Coast oil and gas surge in the early 2010s and the glut of used boats served as the nucleus of the Pentagon’s early autonomous ship experiments.

The Defense Department converted former Gulf Coast crew boats into autonomous test beds and the U.S. Pacific Fleet tested two of the ships in 2023 in the unforgiving waters of the Western Pacific. The Navy used the test results to shape a line of fast, durable ships capable of traveling 2,500 nautical miles, hauling modular payloads camouflaged in two 40-foot shipping containers.

Breaux Brothers has eight father-son duos working in its yard, housed on the property that Brannon Breaux’s family used for summer getaways when he was a child. The company’s current office was once the family vacation home, where young boys played with chickens, donkeys and go-karts outside and jumped from the open second-floor balcony to the first floor couch inside.

“Me and my two brothers would terrorize this place,” Breaux recalled.

Now, he is carrying on the family legacy, running and working at Breaux Brothers with his son.

The yard is one of seven participating in the Navy’s Medium Unmanned Surface Vessel (MUSV) competition, which is currently in the midst of prototype testing expected to wrap by the end of this month.

After years of fits and starts, the Navy is moving out on unmanned ships with the MUSV, which is generating interest from new defense technology startups and legacy shipbuilders alike.

“This MUSV program fits right into our wheelhouse,” said Breaux. “It’s basically a glorified crew boat, or [fast supply vessel]. I mean, it’s a fancier looking one. You’ll see it. It’s sleeker. Now what separates it is the autonomy.”

These Louisiana yards are putting up their own money to pursue unmanned vessels, answering the U.S. government’s call for a so-called marketplace that puts the onus and risk on industry. They also have expansion plans if the U.S. Navy ramps up production and more work comes to the Gulf Coast and Louisiana boat builders.

It’s an area with untapped capacity outside the major defense contractors that have historically constructed the U.S. fleet’s manned warships since World War II.

“We have shipyards in the United States, and those shipyards … when there [were] 3,800 offshore oil and gas platforms in the Gulf of Mexico, which there [were] in the 2010s, they were producing the most advanced OSVs and support vessels and work vessels,” Matt Paxton, the president of the Shipbuilders Council of America, recently told USNI News. “We were exporting those vessels all over the world.”

The Navy has struggled for years to create a strategy to purchase, build and operate an unmanned fleet. But with the evolution of drone warfare and successive administrations focusing on unmanned assets, a hybrid naval fleet is becoming more and more likely. Congress passed a reconciliation bill last year that allotted $5 billion for the Navy to buy unmanned vessels. The service intends to order 36 MUSVs before the end of the current fiscal year, then taper off before increasing purchases again in the outyears.

The smaller shipyards are taking notice.

“We’re building our workforce with the intent of the Navy coming and saying, ‘Don’t stop building,’” Breaux said. “That’s what our intent is. And as soon as they tell us that, we will acquire that piece of land and build whatever it takes to maximize this yard.”

Bots on the Bayou

Forty minutes down Route 90, a four-year-old Austin, Texas-based defense technology startup is erecting new facilities on the same bayou for a 300,000-square-foot expansion.

After purchasing family-owned Gulf Craft in Franklin, La., last year, Saronic is spending $300 million to increase its footprint in anticipation of a hot USV production line for the Navy. Months ago, much of the property that backs up to Bayou Teche was sugar cane fields. Now, two vast buildings that will be fully air-conditioned are taking shape next to the highway.

“We think that there is quite a large MUSV market,” Doug Lambert, Saronic’s chief operating officer, told USNI News during a stop in Franklin.

With the expansion in full swing, excavation equipment was strewn throughout the dirt paths and gravel floors on the humid August day.

Fueled by venture capital, Saronic started in a Texas warehouse building autonomous vessels about 24 feet long – approximately a medium-sized fishing boat. The company has since sold nearly $400 million worth of autonomous vessels to the Navy in 2025 and extended its autonomy suite to a USV more than triple the size.

“We’re primarily building Marauders [at] this site. Incredibly bullish on what that looks like for the future, and then more importantly, we’re seeing use cases that crop up everywhere across the [Department of Defense], to oil and gas, to hydrographic survey,” Lambert said. “The utility of these vessels is quite large. We think that that market’s going to continue to grow, and we continue to invest in it.”

Three MUSVs known as the Marauder, a 180-foot-long aluminum vessel, are currently under construction in Franklin. The first vessel from the Navy’s MUSV marketplace already sailed away for testing.

Of the $5 billion allotted for Navy unmanned systems in last year’s reconciliation bill, $2.1 billion is slated for the MUSV program. The service’s latest shipbuilding outlook projects MUSV purchases increasing over the coming five years, with a goal of buying three in the next fiscal year and 12 by Fiscal Year 2030. Companies like Saronic are preparing to build at that scale, incorporating the Navy’s plans into the new facilities and manufacturing lines.

“You’ll see the traditional Gulf Coast manufacturing process, which is very build-in-place. That’s something that we want to turn the corner around,” Lambert said.

To make that shift, manufacturing lead John Morgan is designing a space so Saronic can meet a serial need should the Navy’s unmanned blueprint come to fruition. Morgan, who formerly worked in manufacturing at Space X, is a proponent of a linear flow. He is crafting the Franklin facility to move material in straight lines so employees can easily identify logjams on the floor.

“Of course we’re going to have all the analytics coming from our manufacturing execution system about throughput, quality, labor hours, all of that will be inherited,” Morgan said. “But also seeing a gap on your floor while you’re getting coffee immediately tells you that you have a problem in a station. You don’t need a computer to tell you that. Within five minutes, everybody should understand what … their top priority for today is – solving that bottleneck that is creating that gap in the system.”

The company has hired around 300 people for the Franklin location since talking over Gulf Craft, which had 29 employees when Saronic bought the yard. The goal is to have 1,500 employees in Franklin when the yard is at full operating capacity. Company executives expect one facility to be finished in October and the other one early next year.

‘They Know How to Speak Navy’

Twenty-seven miles down Route 90, another shipyard that’s been building since the 1940s is teaming up with a young defense startup. On the edge of Cajun Country, Conrad Shipyard boasts four facilities. One is its yard on the Atchafalaya River in Morgan City, where a series of bayous, lakes and rivers drop into the Intracoastal Waterway. Another yard lies 10 minutes away in Amelia. Conrad also has a new construction facility nearby next to a separate deepwater repair yard.

Conrad is partnered with Blue Water Autonomy, a Boston-based company established in 2024 that hired a handful of employees who worked on the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s (DARPA) No Manning Required Ship (NOMARS) program.

“This is a profitable commercial yard … that’s not currently doing a lot of military work,” Ryan Maatta, Blue Water’s head of marine engineering, told USNI News at the Morgan City yard on Front Street.

“But they also pass with flying colors [Supervisors of Shipbuilding] inspection. They know how to speak Navy. It was one of the reasons Blue Water identified them as the best commercial partner for this, and [they] very organically can deliver tens of hulls annually without disrupting or giving up their commercial market.”

The Front Street yard sits behind the city’s steel and concrete storm wall, locally known as the “Great Wall,” built in the 1980s to safeguard against flooding.

Conrad’s commercial portfolio ranges from offshore supply vessels to ferries, but the yard recently entered the naval market with a contract to build the Yard, Repair, Berthing, and Messing barges for the U.S. Navy.

Blue Water and Conrad announced their partnership to build autonomous vessels one year ago. While the Navy chose Blue Water’s USV as one of the contenders for the second phase of the former Modular Attack Surface Craft (MASC) program, the service cancelled MASC in March when it switched to the marketplace acquisition approach. Blue Water competed for the MUSV, the latest iteration of the program, but did not win an award.

Blue Water and Saildrone, which also did not make it to MUSV’s prototyping stage, are currently suing the Navy over the decision. The two companies claim the Navy did not follow its own selection criteria when choosing the awardees.

HII and Saronic made the Navy’s first cut, along with designs from Edison Chouset, Birdon, Leidos, PacMar Technologies and Sea Machines.

But Blue Water and Conrad are still building their steel Liberty USV, a 190-foot vessel based on a Damen-hull parent design.

“We took a proven hull design that we’re confident was heavy weather-capable,” Maatta said. “That hull is known for reduced slamming, high sea-state performance and low resistance without having to do something like aluminum or trimaran or planing, because we don’t think that putting a small vessel at 25 knots in the Pacific is going to work.”

The Navy’s MUSV requirements called for a vessel that could travel at 25 knots for 2,500 nautical miles in sea state 4 while transporting payloads up to 25 metric tons across at least two 40-foot shipping containers.

While commercial maritime companies stepping into the naval market is not new, Navy officials under both the Biden and Trump administrations have voiced a desire to upend shipbuilding acquisition. Both administrations have also excoriated the major defense contractors for their program performance and the practice of stock buybacks.

“There’s a bevy, an ecosystem of small- to mid-sized yards … that have been traditionally underutilized, and that’s fully on the Navy traditionally,” said a senior Department of Navy official. “We’re changing the way we do business 100 percent and that is now a primary focus for the secretary, frankly, at all levels of the administration’s leadership, all the way up to the White House.”

In a maritime action plan released in February, the White House called on the Navy to speed up the operational employment of autonomous vessels. The document specifically identified the Gulf Coast as an area where commercial yards could play a role.

“In short, their production can also be distributed, increasing both competition and shipbuilding capacity while lowering costs,” the plan reads.

But the small yards on the bayous of Acadiana want a sign from the government that it’s committed to serial production before they expand.

Breaux Brothers, which currently employs about 65 people, would like to churn out a boat every two months. The company would increase its workforce by 15-20 employees for that cadence and is eyeing a piece of land next door to grow should the Navy place the orders.

For Brannon Breaux, moving into naval shipbuilding is also personal. When he was younger, he had dreams of becoming a U.S. Marine.

“I watched my father build his business with his brother, and I fell in love with it and I just couldn’t get away from it,” Breaux said. “What you’re seeing here today and what we’re talking about, I can fulfill that dream by giving back to this country and saying, ‘No, I didn’t go in the service. I’m not in harm’s way. But boy, I got something that I can give back to this country and be proud of it.’”

This post has been updated to include that BAE Jacksonville received a $70 million maintenance availability for the Littoral Combat Ship USS Wichita (LCS-13).

VIRGINIA BEACH, Va. — The ongoing U.S. conflict with Iran is morphing how the Navy fixes and supplies ships operating thousands of miles from logistics hubs as extended time at sea and the prospect of an extended naval commitment in the Middle East are creating a maintenance wave back home, service officials said this week.

As of Monday, there were more than a dozen guided-missile destroyers supporting carriers USS George H.W. Bush (CVN-77) and USS George Washington (CVN-73) and the Boxer Amphibious Ready Group in the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean, according to Monday’s USNI News Fleet and Marine Tracker. USS Spruance (DDG-111) and USS McFaul (DDG-74) have been deployed since November – 10 months deployed.

Combined with the expanded U.S. presence in the Red Sea in response to Houthi attacks in 2023, the Navy has been sailing ships into conflict for three years.

“We are sustaining 15 warships in the [weapon engagement zone]. That’s almost four carrier strike groups’ worth of destroyers,” Capt. Eric Kellum, the chief of staff of Naval Surface Force Atlantic, said Wednesday during a panel at the American Society of Naval Engineers Fleet Maintenance and Modernization Symposium.

Now that the Navy has lost access to previous logistics ports, parts and supplies travel from as far away as Diego Garcia – a remote island in the central Indian Ocean – to keep the ships provisioned as the Military Sealift Command has beefed up its presence to keep the fleet moving.

Back in the U.S., the Navy is planning for a wave of maintenance for ships that will return from extended deployments and manage the yards that are currently empty, Adm. Karl Thomas, the commander of U.S. Fleet Forces, said on Wednesday. The Navy has extended deployments for several surface ships and pushed them to U.S. Central Command and, in the case of some, skipped planned maintenance periods, Thomas said.

“For years, when operational commanders were faced with these tough decisions and these urgent operational requirements, the response was often to defer depot maintenance and keep the hull on station,” he said. “The current operational pace has forced us to also address this really difficult decision. But as every naval engineer and every tradesperson in this room knows, you can’t defer maintenance indefinitely without paying the bill.”

To support the buildup in the Middle East, guided-missile destroyers USS Thomas Hudner (DDG-116) and USS Donald Cook (DDG-75) and Littoral Combat Ship USS St. Louis (LCS-19) were extended. Their major maintenance availabilities were pushed from 2026 to 2027.

The shift in availabilities prompted the BAE Systems Jacksonville repair yard to potentially lay off 400 shipyard workers for lack of work. To prevent the loss of workers, the Navy arranged for a $70 million availability for Freedom-class Littoral Combat Ship USS Wichita (LCS-13).

“That emergency intervention was successful, and it averted an immediate disaster,” Thomas said.

But a combination of funding gaps and operational needs has resulted in the cancellation of 18 smaller maintenance periods, Thomas said.

Retired Rear Adm. John Polowczyk, president of the Virginia Ship Repair Association, said the boom-bust cycle has been an issue among the 350 members.

“After [a member] went through his up and down workload demands and numbers of people, he said two things. ‘It’s hard to have a workforce without the work.’ He also said these things could look like bar charts, graphs… It’s somebody’s livelihood,” Polowczyk said. “We don’t necessarily have a workforce problem; we have a workload problem.”

The shifts in availability will surge ships to private repair yards starting in early 2027 and into 2028 – timing that’s less than ideal.

“The current schedule concentrates more than six concurrent availabilities squarely during our peak hurricane season, introducing execution infrastructure and force protection risks,” Thomas said. “This feast or famine dynamic is going to break our shipyards.”

The service is making changes to how it is thinking about maintenance by moving away from major availabilities to instead repairing ships in a way that breaks with longer periods.

“The traditional model of naval ship maintenance is no longer viable in this high-demand operational environment,” Thomas said. “That’s what we [have] got to change.”

The solution is spreading repairs out in a maintenance continuum to prevent all the repairs from piling up in major availabilities, Thomas said.

“The maintenance continuum is a strategic framework designed to maximize fleet readiness through continuous screening, planning and execution across the entire life cycle of a platform. Its core principle is simple: proactively identify and address maintenance needs at the earliest feasible opportunity. Let’s maximize equipment redundancy, extinguish material problems before they cascade into mission-killing casualties,” he said.

To that end, the Navy is trying to push more work down to the sailor level and Shore Intermediate Maintenance Activities have been stood up across the fleet. The SIMAs are designed to develop sailors with elevated repair skills who can supplement the crew and repair yards for work.

Ships in the Middle East are also traveling with more spare parts and are learning to do more repairs at sea, officials said. Additionally, the service is experimenting with new diagnostic tools and generative artificial intelligence to make planning for the availabilities easier.

Officials said that while the supply and maintenance problems have been difficult, the ships have performed well.

“[We’ve had] 1,000 offensive engagements at 97 – almost 98 – percent accuracy and over 300 defensive engagements with zero shots taken. That’s over three years. And believe me, there’s been a lot of attempts,” Kellum said. “I am positive now. I have proof in sustained combat operations. [Sailors] are awesome.”

item.content:encoded:
MANILA, PHILIPPINES – An ex-Taiwan Coast Guard Administration patrol vessel is now under a Philippine flag in the most significant maritime security development between Taipei and Manila in recent years. 

The decommissioned Kinmen, one of four 500-ton Taipei-class patrol vessels commissioned between 2001 and 2008, appeared registered under the Philippines with the name BLING NO.1 on Sept. 16. Maritime tracking website VesselFinder placed the patrol vessel at the Southern Taiwanese port city of Kaohsiung, home to the bulk of Taipei’s Navy and Coast Guard vessels. 

The Coast Guard Administration of Taiwan clarified last week that the vessel transfer was based on the precedent of previous donations of retired patrol ships to partners such as the Marshall Islands, Palau and Tuvalu. Another statement from the maritime security agency on Sept. 20 said the transfer agreement stipulates that the former cutter “will never be used for law enforcement against Taiwanese fishing vessels.” 

This week, the West Philippine Sea (WPS) Foundation officially handed over the deed of ownership of the vessel to the Philippine Coast Guard in Manila. The Tuesday ceremony revealed that ex-Kinmen will be used for training purposes and missions around Mindanao, a Southern Philippine island located away from the South China Sea and Luzon Strait. 

All crew-served weaponry was removed before its transfer to Philippine service, according to media released by the WPS Foundation. 

The Taiwanese-origin training ship transfer comes ahead of the Philippine Coast Guard’s planned 45 patrol vessel procurement plan. In the coming years, the service will receive 40 patrol boats from France and five cutters from Japan through loan assistance schemes. 

“This donation is about saving lives, protecting our seas and building the capacity of the men and women of the Philippine Coast Guard. We are proud to have turned over a platform that will serve Filipino fishermen, mariners and coastal communities,” said Jeffrey Ordaniel, president and CEO of the WPS Foundation, in a social media post. 

The nonprofit handling the transfer has previously hosted numerous conferences advocating for Philippine claims in the South China Sea, specifically within the western exclusive economic zone waters that comprises its namesake. Kinmen’s Taiwanese origins were not highlighted in the WPS Foundation’s release. However, photos on Ordaniel’s social media page showcased the initial inspection of the vessel at Kaohsiung at an unspecified date. 

Google Earth imagery shows that Kinmen appeared at the location of the foundation’s visit between April and June of this year. 

A Philippine government source granted anonymity to speak to USNI News said that Taipei sent a list of vessels – including Coast Guard Administration patrol ships – to Manila in between 2022 and 2024 during the early years of Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s presidency. It is unclear whether the transfer of Kinmen was as a result of this list or if any ships were selected by the Philippine government. 

In 2027, Taipei plans to send up to 100 Coast Guard personnel to the Philippines for a goodwill mission. 

The nature of the transfer between Taipei and Manila through a non-governmental organization highlights the slowly, and silently, growing cooperation in defense and security. This work has been increasing amid mutual threats from China and concerns of how a cross strait conflict may impact the broader region.

item.content:encoded:
North Korea test launched a new weapon over the weekend that appears to be a hypersonic missile, according to photos released Tuesday by state media Korean Central News Agency.

North Korea’s Missile Administration Bureau tested a new weapon on Sunday, demonstrating the rapid technological development of the weapon systems, KCNA reported.

KCNA did not specify what the weapons were but wording on a display of the missile’s movement reads: “Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 flight trajectory,” indicating an upgraded version of the Hwasong-11MA hypersonic missiles that North Korea unveiled last year. Additionally, imagery shows the fired missiles having the sharp dart-like tip of hypersonic missiles, rather than the blunt cone tip of ballistic missiles.

“Today’s success is the priceless fruit brought by a special force of the sci-tech group involved in the development of this important weapon system for a specific purpose and their devoted efforts,” said North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, who oversaw the tests, according to a Pyongyang Times report.

Kim’s remarks indicated that North Korea has completed its research into hypersonic missile technology and is now moving towards deploying the missiles operationally. North Korea test fired the hypersonic missiles in October last year, USNI News reported.

The test did not have any adverse impact on the security of neighboring countries and is an extension of the regular activities of the Missile Administration and its defense science research institutes aimed at implementing the national defense policy, KCNA reported.

KCNA did not disclose how many missiles were launched, the location of the launch or performance details of the missiles but South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) and Japan’s Ministry of Defense provided estimates on Sunday.

According to South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff, North Korea fired two missiles from the Wonsan area towards the Sea of Japan on Sunday.

The first missile was launched at 3 p.m. local time and the second at 5:50 p.m. The first missile traveled 450 kilometers – around 280 miles – and the second traveled more than 600 kilometers – 373 miles.

South Korea and the U.S. are currently conducting an analysis of the missile’s exact specifications.

“Under a firm ROK-U.S. combined defense posture, our military is closely monitoring various North Korean movements and maintaining the capability and readiness to respond overwhelmingly to any provocation,” reads the JCS statement.

Japan’s Ministry of Defense issued two reports on the missile launch, confirming the timing of the launches.

Japan estimated that the first missile reached a maximum altitude of 60 kilometers – 37 miles – and flew for 440 kilometers –273 miles – before landing outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone in the Sea of ​​Japan.

The second report said the missile launched around 5:50 p.m. t reached a maximum altitude of 70 kilometers – 43 miles – flew for about 590 kilometers – 367 miles – before it landed outside of Japan’s EEZ.

North Korea has launched at least 15 ballistic missiles and other projectiles on nine occasions since the start of 2026 in contrast to last year’s total of five missiles on four occasions, Japan Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said in an X post on Sunday. Koizumi stated that Japan has lodged a strong protest and condemnation of North Korea through North Korea’s embassy in Beijing.

In a Sunday press conference, Koizumi was asked on North Korea’s intentions for the launches and replied that it was difficult to give a definitive answer regarding the intentions behind each individual launch by North Korea.

“However, whatever their objectives may be, North Korea’s nuclear and missile development threatens the peace and stability of Japan and the international community, and violates relevant Security Council resolutions, and is absolutely unacceptable,” Koizumi said.
